items.prompt: Where did Dilnoza and Jasur travel to?
items.passage:
Last July, Dilnoza and her younger brother Jasur took a ferry from Barcelona to the island of Mallorca. They had never travelled on a big boat before, so they were very excited. The ferry left at ten o'clock in the evening, and the journey was going to take about eight hours.

When they arrived at the port, there was a long queue of cars and lorries. Dilnoza showed the tickets to a man in a yellow jacket, and he told them to wait near gate four. The tickets cost sixty-five euros each, which was cheaper than the plane, but the plane was much faster. Dilnoza said that a night on the sea would be more interesting than a short flight.

Inside the ferry, there were two restaurants, a small shop and a cinema. Jasur wanted to watch a film, but Dilnoza was tired, so they found their cabin on deck six. It was small, with two beds and one round window. Jasur put his bag on the top bed and said that he would sleep there.

At midnight the sea became rough. The ferry moved from side to side, and Jasur felt sick. Dilnoza took him to the open deck, where the fresh air helped him. They sat there for an hour and watched the lights of a fishing boat far away. A kind sailor named Mr Garcia gave Jasur a cup of ginger tea and told him to look at the horizon.

By four o'clock the weather was calmer, and both of them slept well. In the morning they woke up when the captain made an announcement. The ferry was going to arrive in Palma at six thirty. Dilnoza and Jasur stood on the deck and watched the sun rise over the mountains. Jasur said that he had changed his mind about boats. Next summer he wants to take a ferry to Italy, but he has promised to buy sea-sickness tablets first.

items.prompt: How long did Madina stay in Rome?
items.passage:
Madina was twenty-four when she went to Rome for a short holiday. She stayed for four days with her friend Elena, and they visited the Colosseum, the Trevi Fountain and many small cafes. On Friday evening, Madina was going to fly home at nine o'clock, so she packed her suitcase and took a taxi to the airport at five.

At the check-in desk, the young woman asked for her passport. Madina opened her bag, but it was not there. She looked in every pocket twice. Her heart was beating fast. She remembered that she had used the passport at lunchtime to pay for a museum ticket, and after that she had visited a cafe near the Pantheon.

Madina rang Elena, who told her to stay calm. Elena called the cafe, and a waiter called Marco answered the phone. He said that a customer had found a red passport under a chair and given it to him. Marco promised to keep it safe, but the cafe was in the city centre, and the traffic was heavy at that time of day.

Madina took a second taxi back to the centre. It was slower than she hoped, and the journey lasted fifty minutes. When she finally arrived, Marco was standing at the door with the passport in his hand. She thanked him and gave him twenty euros, but he only smiled and said that he was happy to help.

Sadly, Madina missed her flight, and the next one to Tashkent was on Saturday morning. She stayed one more night at Elena's flat and paid a small fee to change her ticket. Now she always keeps her passport in an inside pocket with a zip, and she takes a photo of it before every trip. She says that this adventure taught her to be more careful.

items.prompt: Where did the friends go camping?
items.passage:
Timur and three friends decided to spend a weekend camping at Lake Charvak, about eighty kilometres from Tashkent. They left the city early on Saturday morning in Timur's old blue car. The road was busy, so the journey took two hours, which was longer than they expected.

At the lake, they chose a flat place under some tall trees, near the water. Together they put up two tents. It was harder than it looked, because the wind was strong and the instructions were in German. After an hour, however, both tents were standing, and the boys were proud of their work.

In the afternoon they swam in the lake. The water was colder than the air, but it was clean and beautiful. Then Bekzod, who was the best cook, started to prepare dinner. He wanted to make a big soup with potatoes, carrots and meat. Unfortunately, nobody had brought matches, and they could not light the fire.

Timur walked to a small shop near the road. He was lucky, because the shop was still open. He bought two boxes of matches and a bag of bread for the evening. When he came back, it was getting dark, and the soup was ready in half an hour. They all agreed that it was the best meal of the year.

At night it started to rain. The water came into one tent, and two boys had to move into the other one. Nobody slept very well, but in the morning the sun was shining again. They ate bread and cheese for breakfast, packed their bags and cleaned the place carefully. Next time, Timur has promised to bring a bigger tent, a torch and a lot more matches, because he never wants to forget them again.

items.prompt: How many nights did the couple book?
items.passage:
Mr Brown and his wife Linda arrived at the Hotel Sunrise in Antalya on a hot Tuesday afternoon. They had booked a room with a sea view for seven nights, and the price was four hundred and fifty pounds. At first, the receptionist was polite, and the lobby looked clean and modern. However, the problems began when they opened the door of room 312.

The air conditioning did not work, and the room was very hot. There was also no sea view. The window looked at a car park and a building site. Mr Brown phoned the reception desk, and a man promised to send someone to repair the air conditioning in ten minutes. Nobody came for two hours.

That night was even worse. The builders started work at six in the morning, and the noise woke the couple up. Linda had not slept well, and she was angry. She said that the hotel was worse than the one they had stayed in last year in Greece. After breakfast, Mr Brown went to the reception desk and asked to speak to the manager.

The manager, Ms Kaya, listened carefully. She apologised and said that the hotel was full of guests that week. She offered them a bigger room on the fifth floor, with a balcony and a real view of the sea. She also gave them a twenty percent discount and two free dinners in the hotel restaurant.

Mr Brown was surprised that she solved the problem so quickly. They moved their bags at noon, and the new room was quiet, cool and bright. In the end, the couple enjoyed their holiday. Before they left, Linda wrote a short review on the internet. She said that the beginning was bad, but the manager was excellent and she would visit again.

items.prompt: What did Nodira eat for breakfast?
items.passage:
Nodira had only one day in Istanbul, so she made a plan the night before. She was staying near Taksim Square, and she wanted to see as much as possible. At eight o'clock she ate a simit, a round bread with sesame seeds, and drank a glass of tea. Then she took the tram to the old city.

Her first stop was the Blue Mosque. It was bigger than she imagined, and the inside was full of blue tiles. She had to take off her shoes and cover her hair, but the guard was friendly and explained everything in simple English. Across the square she visited Hagia Sophia. The queue was long, and she waited forty minutes. She thought it was worth it, because the building was nearly fifteen hundred years old.

At noon she was hungry. She found a small restaurant and ordered a kebab with rice and salad. It cost less than she had expected, only eight dollars. After lunch she walked to the Grand Bazaar, where there are more than four thousand shops. She bought a blue bowl for her mother and a scarf for her sister. A seller told her the price was two hundred lira, but she said that it was too expensive, and he lowered it to a hundred and fifty.

In the late afternoon she took a ferry across the Bosphorus to the Asian side. The boat ride lasted twenty minutes, and the view of the city was wonderful. Seagulls followed the ferry, and she fed them pieces of bread.

In the evening she climbed the Galata Tower and watched the sunset. The sky turned orange and pink. Nodira was tired, but she felt very happy. She promised herself that she would come back to Istanbul for a whole week, because one day was not enough.

items.prompt: Where did Sherzod go skiing?
items.passage:
Last winter, Sherzod went to Austria with his school friends for a week of skiing. He was fifteen, and he had never seen so much snow in his life. They stayed in a small wooden hotel in the village of Zell am See, and every morning a bus took them to the mountain at nine o'clock.

On the first day, the group had a lesson with an instructor named Hans. He was tall, funny and very patient. Hans taught them how to stand on skis, how to turn and, most importantly, how to stop. Sherzod found it difficult. He fell over eleven times in the first hour, and his friend Aziz laughed at him. Sherzod was embarrassed, but he did not give up.

On the second day, he felt more confident. The weather was perfect, with blue sky and no wind. Hans took the group up the lift to a longer slope. Halfway down, Sherzod went too fast and crashed into a pile of soft snow. He was not hurt, but he lost one ski, and it took ten minutes to find it. That afternoon he sat in the mountain cafe and drank hot chocolate with the others.

By Thursday, Sherzod could ski down the easy slope without falling. He was prouder than ever. On Friday there was a small race, and he came fourth out of twelve people. Aziz won, but Sherzod did not mind, because he had improved a lot in only five days.

On Saturday morning the friends packed their bags and said goodbye to Hans. The week was expensive, about nine hundred euros, but Sherzod says it was worth every cent. Next year he would like to try snowboarding, which looks even more difficult than skiing.

Last winter, Sherzod went to Austria with his school friends for a week of skiing. He was fifteen, and he had never seen so much snow in his life. They stayed in a small wooden hotel in the village of Zell am See, and every morning a bus took them to the mountain at nine o'clock.

On the first day, the group had a lesson with an instructor named Hans. He was tall, funny and very patient. Hans taught them how to stand on skis, how to turn and, most importantly, how to stop. Sherzod found it difficult. He fell over eleven times in the first hour, and his friend Aziz laughed at him. Sherzod was embarrassed, but he did not give up.

On the second day, he felt more confident. The weather was perfect, with blue sky and no wind. Hans took the group up the lift to a longer slope. Halfway down, Sherzod went too fast and crashed into a pile of soft snow. He was not hurt, but he lost one ski, and it took ten minutes to find it. That afternoon he sat in the mountain cafe and drank hot chocolate with the others.

By Thursday, Sherzod could ski down the easy slope without falling. He was prouder than ever. On Friday there was a small race, and he came fourth out of twelve people. Aziz won, but Sherzod did not mind, because he had improved a lot in only five days.

On Saturday morning the friends packed their bags and said goodbye to Hans. The week was expensive, about nine hundred euros, but Sherzod says it was worth every cent. Next year he would like to try snowboarding, which looks even more difficult than skiing.

items.prompt: Where was Kamola going?
items.answer: To Bukhara to visit her grandmother
items.passage:
Kamola had never taken a night train before, so she was both nervous and excited. She was going from Tashkent to Bukhara to visit her grandmother, and the train left at nine in the evening. The journey was going to take about seven hours, and her ticket for the second-class carriage cost one hundred and ten thousand sum.

When she found her compartment, there were already three people inside. An old man called Rustam was sitting by the window, a young mother was holding a sleeping baby, and a student was reading a book on the top bed. Kamola's bed was in the middle. It was narrower than she expected, but the blanket was warm, and the sheets smelled fresh.

After an hour, the old man opened his bag and took out a flask of green tea and some bread with sesame seeds. He asked Kamola if she wanted some, and she said yes with a smile. They talked for a long time. Rustam said that he had worked on trains for thirty years. He told her about a snowstorm in 1998, when his train stopped for nine hours in the middle of the desert.

Around midnight, the lights went off and everyone tried to sleep. The train moved from side to side, and the wheels made a loud and regular noise. Kamola woke up twice, but she liked the feeling. It was quite different from a plane or a bus.

At four o'clock in the morning, the train arrived in Bukhara, about twenty minutes late. Kamola said goodbye to Rustam, who gave her a small packet of dried apricots for her grandmother. Her grandmother was waiting on the platform in a thick coat. Kamola decided that she would take the night train again, because it was cheaper than flying and much more fun.

items.prompt: Why was Oliver going to Dubai?
items.passage:
Oliver was going to Dubai for a business meeting. His flight from London was planned for seven in the morning, so he arrived at the airport at four thirty. He checked in his small suitcase, went through security and bought a coffee. Everything was going well until he looked at the big screen and saw the word DELAYED next to his flight.

A woman at the information desk explained the problem. There was thick fog over the airport, and no plane could take off. She said that the delay might last two hours, but nobody knew for sure. Oliver sent a message to his manager and sat down near gate twenty-two.

Two hours later, the screen showed a new time: noon. Then it changed again, to one thirty. In total, Oliver waited almost seven hours. The airline gave every passenger a lunch voucher worth twelve pounds. He ate a sandwich and a salad, and he spent the rest of the money on a bottle of water and a magazine.

While he was waiting, he met a young doctor called Sara. She was flying to Dubai to see her brother, and she was more worried than Oliver, because her phone battery was nearly empty. Oliver lent her his charger, and in return she shared her chocolate. They talked about work, travel and their favourite cities. Time passed more quickly than he had thought.

Finally, at two o'clock, the fog disappeared and the passengers boarded the plane. The flight lasted seven hours. Oliver missed his meeting, but his manager was understanding and moved it to the next day. He told Sara that he would never again travel without a book, a charger and a bit of patience.

A woman at the information desk explained the problem. There was thick fog over the airport, and no plane could take off. She said that the delay might last two hours, but nobody knew for sure. Oliver sent a message to his manager and sat down near gate twenty-two.

Two hours later, the screen showed a new time: noon. Then it changed again, to one thirty. In total, Oliver waited almost seven hours. The airline gave every passenger a lunch voucher worth twelve pounds. He ate a sandwich and a salad, and he spent the rest of the money on a bottle of water and a magazine.

While he was waiting, he met a young doctor called Sara. She was flying to Dubai to see her brother, and she was more worried than Oliver, because her phone battery was nearly empty. Oliver lent her his charger, and in return she shared her chocolate. They talked about work, travel and their favourite cities. Time passed more quickly than he had thought.

Finally, at two o'clock, the fog disappeared and the passengers boarded the plane. The flight lasted seven hours. Oliver missed his meeting, but his manager was understanding and moved it to the next day. He told Sara that he would never again travel without a book, a charger and a bit of patience.

items.prompt: Where did the girls start their road trip?
items.passage:
Laylo and her cousin Anna dreamed about a road trip for years. Last August they finally flew to San Francisco and rented a small red car. Their plan was to drive south along Highway One for five days, about eight hundred kilometres in total, and finish in Los Angeles.

On the first morning, they left the city at eight o'clock. The weather was cool and foggy, but after lunch the sun came out. The road went along high cliffs, and the sea was far below them. They stopped many times to take photos. In a small town called Monterey, they visited an aquarium and watched a big group of jellyfish. Laylo said that it was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen.

On the second day, Anna drove for six hours and began to feel tired. They found a cheap motel near Big Sur and had pizza for dinner. In the night, they heard a strange noise outside. In the morning they saw that a family of raccoons had opened their food bag and eaten all the biscuits. The girls laughed for ten minutes.

The third and fourth days were easier. They visited a famous castle and swam in the ocean, which was colder than they had imagined. They also listened to music, sang loudly and argued about which radio station was better.

On the last day, they were stuck in traffic for two hours near Los Angeles. Anna was bored and impatient, but Laylo stayed calm. When they returned the car, the man at the rental office told them that they had driven exactly nine hundred and twelve kilometres. They were tired but happy, and already planning the next trip, perhaps across Italy.

items.prompt: How high is the mountain hut?
items.passage:
Bobur and his father love the mountains. Last September they decided to walk to a mountain hut in the Fann Mountains in Tajikistan. The hut stands at two thousand eight hundred metres above the sea, and the walk from the road takes about five hours. Bobur was twelve, and it was his first long hike.

They started at seven in the morning. At the beginning the path was easy, but after two hours it became steeper and rockier. Bobur carried a small rucksack with water, an apple and a warm jumper. His father carried a bigger one with their sleeping bags. They rested every hour, and in the middle of the day they ate bread and cheese next to a clear blue stream.

At three o'clock in the afternoon they reached the hut. It was a simple wooden building with one big room and fifteen beds. A friendly woman called Mrs Saidova welcomed them with hot tea. She told them that there was no electricity or mobile phone signal, only candles. Bobur thought that this was strange, but he soon found it interesting.

For dinner, everyone ate a thick soup with potatoes and mutton. A group of German walkers sat at the next table and showed Bobur a map of the area. They said that the next day's walk would be harder than the first one, but the view from the top was incredible.

That night it was very cold, and there were more stars in the sky than Bobur had ever seen. He slept badly because a man in the next bed was snoring loudly. At five thirty he got up and watched the sun rise over the peaks. His father put an arm around him and said that he was proud of him.

items.passage:
For their fortieth wedding anniversary, Mr and Mrs Evans from Manchester booked a river cruise on the Danube. They had always wanted to see Vienna, Bratislava and Budapest, and a boat seemed more relaxing than a train. The trip lasted six days, and it cost three thousand pounds for two people.

They arrived at the ship on a sunny Sunday. It was smaller than they imagined, with only eighty cabins, but it was clean and comfortable. Their cabin had a large window, so they could watch the river from their bed. The captain, a cheerful Austrian named Mr Huber, shook hands with every passenger at the door.

On Monday morning the ship left Vienna. Mrs Evans spent the day on the top deck with a book, while her husband talked to a retired teacher from Canada. In the afternoon the boat passed through a narrow valley with castles on both sides of the river. Mr Evans took more than a hundred photographs.

In Bratislava, the group joined a walking tour. The guide was a young woman who spoke fast, and Mrs Evans could not understand everything. After the tour, they sat in a small cafe and ate a delicious cake with plums and cream. Mr Evans said that it was better than anything in England, and his wife agreed.

On the last evening in Budapest, the ship organised a special dinner with live music. The couple danced for the first time in ten years. They felt a little silly, but the other passengers clapped. Mrs Evans said that it was the best holiday of her life, and she is already looking at brochures for a cruise on the Rhine next year.

items.prompt: How long did Emma stay in Thailand?
items.passage:
Hello, travel friends! I am Emma, and last month I spent three weeks in Thailand. It was my first trip to Asia, and I made a few mistakes. Here are my five best tips for you, so you do not repeat them.

Tip number one: pack light. I took a huge suitcase with twenty kilos of clothes, and I wore only a quarter of them. The weather is hot, so shorts and T-shirts are enough. Buy a cheap umbrella when you arrive, because it rains almost every afternoon in the wet season.

Tip number two: eat street food. I was afraid at first, but it was cheaper, fresher and tastier than the hotel restaurants. A big plate of noodles cost about one dollar. My favourite meal was mango with sticky rice. Just choose busy stalls, because the food there is usually the freshest.

Tip number three: use the local transport. In Bangkok, the Skytrain is quicker than a taxi when the traffic is bad. In the north, I travelled by night bus from the capital to Chiang Mai. It took ten hours, and the seats were more comfortable than I expected.

Tip number four: respect the culture. When you visit a temple, cover your shoulders and knees, and take off your shoes. Never touch a person's head, and always smile. Thai people are very kind, and a smile can solve many problems.

Tip number five: slow down. On my last week, I stayed on a small island called Koh Lanta and did absolutely nothing. I swam, read three books and watched the sunset every night. It was the best part of my trip. I will definitely return next year, and this time I will learn some Thai words before I go.

items.prompt: Where did the tour finish?
items.passage:
Dilshod had never been on a long cycling holiday, but last May he joined a tour in the Netherlands with his friend Jack. The route went from Amsterdam to the town of Maastricht, a distance of about three hundred and sixty kilometres. They planned to cycle sixty kilometres a day for six days and sleep in small guest houses.

The first day was perfect. The land was flat, the sky was blue, and cyclists had their own paths everywhere. They passed green fields, windmills and hundreds of cows. Dilshod noticed that the Dutch ride bicycles more than any people he had met. Even grandmothers in elegant dresses were faster than him.

On the second day, the wind was against them. It was so strong that they moved at only ten kilometres an hour. Dilshod felt exhausted, and his legs were sore. Jack suggested a long coffee break, and they ate two pieces of apple pie in a village cafe. After that, Dilshod felt better.

On the third day, Dilshod got a puncture. He had a spare tube, but he did not know how to change it. A friendly farmer stopped his tractor and helped. It took only fifteen minutes, and the farmer refused any money. Dilshod decided to watch a video about bicycle repair that evening.

items.prompt: What did Kate and Dan most want to see?
items.answer: Waterfalls, glaciers and the Northern Lights
items.passage:
Kate and her husband Dan flew to Iceland for a week in March. They wanted to see waterfalls, glaciers and, if they were lucky, the Northern Lights. At the airport they went to a car rental office, where a young man named Siggi gave them the keys to a small white car. It was the cheapest one, at forty pounds a day.

Siggi asked them if they would like to pay for extra insurance. Kate said no, because she thought it was too expensive. Siggi explained that the weather in Iceland changes quickly, and that stones and strong wind often damage cars. In the end, they agreed to take the insurance, which cost another ten pounds a day. Later, they were very glad about this decision.

On the second day, they drove east along the south coast. The road was good, and the scenery was fantastic. They stopped at a waterfall, which was taller than any building Kate had ever seen. Then they visited a black beach and took many photographs. Dan wanted to drive on a gravel road to a hidden lake, but Kate was nervous, so they stayed on the main road.

On the fourth day, the wind became so strong that it nearly blew the car door off. Dan opened it, and the wind pushed it hard against a fence. There was a big scratch, but thanks to the insurance they paid nothing. They also had to stop on the road because a group of sheep was crossing slowly, and nobody was in a hurry.

On the last night, the sky was clear, and green lights moved above them. Kate and Dan stood in the cold for an hour. When they returned the car, Siggi smiled and asked if they would come back. They answered yes without thinking.
options: Waterfalls, glaciers and the Northern Lights

items.prompt: Where was the family staying?
items.answer: In a small hotel near King's Cross
items.passage:
Anvar, his wife Zulfiya and their two children spent a rainy Saturday in London last April. They were staying in a small hotel near King's Cross station, and they had only one day for sightseeing. The children, Malika and Eldor, were nine and six, and they wanted to see everything.

They began the morning with a ride on a red double-decker bus. The children sat on the top floor at the front, and Eldor pretended to drive. The bus was slower than the underground, but the view of the streets was more interesting. They passed Big Ben, the Houses of Parliament and a large crowd of tourists with umbrellas.

At eleven o'clock they reached the Tower of London. A guide in a red uniform told them about the kings and queens who had lived there. Malika was especially excited about the crown jewels, which were shining under bright lights. Eldor liked the ravens, the large black birds that live in the tower. The guide said that if the ravens ever leave, the kingdom will fall.

Lunch was in a cheap pub, where the family ordered fish and chips. Anvar thought that the portions were enormous, and he could not finish his meal. After lunch the rain stopped, and they walked along the river to the London Eye. The queue was fifty minutes long, but the ride was fantastic. From the top, they could see the whole city.

In the evening everyone was exhausted. Eldor fell asleep on the underground, and Anvar carried him back to the hotel. On Sunday morning, Zulfiya said that one day had been too short and that they would visit again in the summer, when the weather would be better.

In a small hotel near King's Cross

They began the morning with a ride on a red double-decker bus. The children sat on the top floor at the front, and Eldor pretended to drive. The bus was slower than the underground, but the view of the streets was more interesting. They passed Big Ben, the Houses of Parliament and a large crowd of tourists with umbrellas.

At eleven o'clock they reached the Tower of London. A guide in a red uniform told them about the kings and queens who had lived there. Malika was especially excited about the crown jewels, which were shining under bright lights. Eldor liked the ravens, the large black birds that live in the tower. The guide said that if the ravens ever leave, the kingdom will fall.

Lunch was in a cheap pub, where the family ordered fish and chips. Anvar thought that the portions were enormous, and he could not finish his meal. After lunch the rain stopped, and they walked along the river to the London Eye. The queue was fifty minutes long, but the ride was fantastic. From the top, they could see the whole city.

In the evening everyone was exhausted. Eldor fell asleep on the underground, and Anvar carried him back to the hotel. On Sunday morning, Zulfiya said that one day had been too short and that they would visit again in the summer, when the weather would be better.

items.prompt: What time did Dilnoza wake up on Monday?
items.passage:
Dilnoza woke up at six o'clock on Monday because it was her first day at a new job. She was going to work at the front desk of a language school in Tashkent. She was very nervous, so she could not eat much breakfast.

The school was twenty minutes away by bus. When she arrived at eight thirty, her manager, Mr Karimov, was waiting at the door. "Welcome," he said. "Today you will not do anything difficult. You will meet the teachers and learn how the computer system works." Dilnoza felt better at once.

First, Mr Karimov showed her the building. There were twelve classrooms on three floors, and a small library next to the kitchen. Then he introduced her to a teacher called Sarah, who came from Canada. Sarah gave her a cup of coffee and a short list of the most common questions that students ask. "Answer slowly and smile," she said. "That is the secret."

At ten o'clock, a student came to the desk and asked about the price of an evening course. Dilnoza was looking at the screen when she suddenly forgot everything. Luckily, Sarah was passing and helped her find the answer. The course cost four hundred thousand soums for two months.

At one o'clock, everybody had lunch together in the kitchen. Dilnoza sat next to a young accountant named Bobur, who had worked at the school for three years. He told her that his first day had been much worse. He had lost the keys to the main door and the whole school had waited outside in the rain for an hour.

In the afternoon, Dilnoza answered the telephone four times and wrote down two new students' names without any mistakes. At five thirty, Mr Karimov thanked her and said she had done a good job. On the bus home, Dilnoza was tired but happy. She decided that tomorrow she would bring a proper lunch and arrive ten minutes early.

items.passage:
Rustam is a bus driver in Samarkand. He drives bus number forty-two, and his working day starts very early. His alarm rings at four thirty, and by five fifteen he is at the bus station, checking the tyres, the lights and the doors. Every morning he also cleans the front window himself because he likes to see the road clearly.

The first bus leaves at six o'clock. At that time there are only a few passengers: workers, a couple of students and an old woman who goes to the market every day. Rustam knows all of them by name. The busiest time is between seven thirty and nine, when the bus carries almost sixty people. "It is like a small moving town," he says, laughing.

The route is eighteen kilometres long and has thirty stops. A full trip takes about fifty minutes, but in winter it is slower because of snow and fog. Rustam says the hardest part of the job is not the traffic. It is being patient with people who shout when the bus is late. He always answers in a quiet voice, and usually the passenger calms down.

At twelve thirty he has a lunch break for forty minutes. He eats bread and soup in a small cafe near the station and phones his daughter, Madina, who is seven. She is learning to read, and every day she reads him one page from her book.

Last month something unusual happened. A young man left a bag on the bus with an expensive laptop inside. Rustam found it at the end of the route and drove straight to the police station. The next day the owner came to say thank you and gave him a box of sweets.

Rustam finishes work at three thirty. He has been a driver for eleven years and does not want to change his job. "I meet hundreds of people every day," he says. "How many office workers can say that?" On Sundays he rests and takes his family to the park.

items.prompt: How much land does Aziz have?
items.passage:
Aziz is a farmer in the Fergana Valley. He has twelve hectares of land, where he grows wheat, tomatoes and apples. For him, every season brings different work, and he says a farmer never really has a holiday.

The year begins in February, when the weather is still cold. Aziz repairs his tractor and buys seeds. In March, he plants the tomatoes in small greenhouses, so they can grow before the frost ends. At the same time, he cuts the old branches of his apple trees. This is difficult work, but it helps the trees to give more fruit.

In April and May, the busiest weeks begin. He sows the wheat and waters the fields every three days. His two sons, Jasur and Sardor, help him after school. Last spring there was a problem: heavy rain fell for a week and the water covered one corner of the field. Aziz dug a small canal, and the water ran away. He was lucky because nothing was lost.

Summer is hot, sometimes more than forty degrees. Aziz starts at five in the morning and stops at eleven, because the afternoon sun is too strong. In June he harvests the wheat with a rented machine. In July the tomatoes are ready, and his wife, Gulnora, sells them at the local market. The best day of the year, she says, is when the first red tomatoes appear.

Autumn is for apples. Aziz picks about nine tons every year and sells most of them to a juice factory. Then he plants new wheat for the next year. Winter is quieter. He rests, fixes his tools and plans the next season with his sons.

Last year was not easy. Prices were low, and the summer was very dry. But Aziz is not afraid of the future. "The land always gives you something back," he says. "You only have to be patient and work hard." This year he wants to buy a second tractor and start a small shop at the market.

items.prompt: What did Malika want to be when she was young?
items.passage:
Malika is a chef in a busy restaurant in Bukhara. She was not always a cook. When she was young, she wanted to be a nurse, but at nineteen she worked in her uncle's small cafe for a summer and fell in love with cooking. Now she is thirty-four and has been head chef for four years.

Her day starts at seven in the morning, long before the restaurant opens. First, she visits the market to buy fresh vegetables, meat and herbs. "A good tomato needs only salt," she says. Then she returns to the kitchen, where eight cooks are already cutting and boiling.

Lunch is served from twelve to three, and dinner from six to eleven. During these hours, the kitchen is hot, loud and very fast. Malika stands in the middle and shouts the orders. If a plate is not perfect, she sends it back. Some young cooks are afraid of her at first, but they soon understand that she is strict because she wants everyone to improve.

The restaurant's most famous dish is plov with lamb and yellow carrots, which takes three hours to prepare. Tourists from many countries ask for it, and last year a famous travel magazine from Germany wrote about it. After that article, the restaurant got twice as many guests, and Malika had to hire three new cooks.

There is one problem with her job: she rarely sees her family in the evening. Her husband, Anvar, works in a bank, and they usually have dinner together only on Mondays, when the restaurant is closed. On those days Malika never cooks. Anvar makes simple pasta, and she says it is the best meal of the week.

In the future, Malika would like to open her own restaurant and a small cooking school for young people who have no money for expensive courses. She has already found a building. Now she is saving money, and she hopes to open the doors next spring.

items.prompt: What is Otabek studying?
items.passage:
Last Saturday, Otabek went to a job fair at his university. He is twenty-two and he finishes his studies in computer science in June. He wanted to find a job before the summer, so he woke up early and put on his only suit, which was a little too big for him.

The fair was in the sports hall, and more than forty companies had small tables there. Some were big banks and phone companies, and others were new, small firms with only ten workers. Otabek arrived at nine o'clock, but there was already a long line at the door. He waited for twenty minutes and then received a map and a free bag with a pen inside.

First, he visited a software company called BrightLine. A young woman named Zilola talked to him about their programmers. She said that the company looked for people who learn fast, not only for people with perfect marks. She took his paper with his name and phone number, and she promised to call him in two weeks.

Then Otabek joined a short talk about writing a good CV. The speaker, a man from a recruitment agency, said that a CV must be shorter than two pages and should never have spelling mistakes. Otabek looked at his own CV and found one mistake in the first line. He laughed and corrected it with a pen.

At noon he was hungry, but the cafe was too expensive, so he ate a sandwich outside with a friend, Kamila. She was looking for a job in tourism. They compared their lists and decided to visit three more tables together.

By three o'clock, Otabek had spoken to eight companies and collected a lot of advice. He felt tired but hopeful. On Monday, BrightLine called him earlier than promised and invited him to an interview on Thursday. He was very excited and started to prepare his answers that evening.

Last Saturday, Otabek went to a job fair at his university. He is twenty-two and he finishes his studies in computer science in June. He wanted to find a job before the summer, so he woke up early and put on his only suit, which was a little too big for him.

The fair was in the sports hall, and more than forty companies had small tables there. Some were big banks and phone companies, and others were new, small firms with only ten workers. Otabek arrived at nine o'clock, but there was already a long line at the door. He waited for twenty minutes and then received a map and a free bag with a pen inside.

First, he visited a software company called BrightLine. A young woman named Zilola talked to him about their programmers. She said that the company looked for people who learn fast, not only for people with perfect marks. She took his paper with his name and phone number, and she promised to call him in two weeks.

Then Otabek joined a short talk about writing a good CV. The speaker, a man from a recruitment agency, said that a CV must be shorter than two pages and should never have spelling mistakes. Otabek looked at his own CV and found one mistake in the first line. He laughed and corrected it with a pen.

At noon he was hungry, but the cafe was too expensive, so he ate a sandwich outside with a friend, Kamila. She was looking for a job in tourism. They compared their lists and decided to visit three more tables together.

By three o'clock, Otabek had spoken to eight companies and collected a lot of advice. He felt tired but hopeful. On Monday, BrightLine called him earlier than promised and invited him to an interview on Thursday. He was very excited and started to prepare his answers that evening.

items.prompt: In which town does Sevara go to school?
items.passage:
Sevara is seventeen and goes to high school in Namangan. Three months ago she started a part-time job at a small bookshop near her house. She works on Wednesdays after school and all day on Saturdays, and she earns about thirty thousand soums every day.

She wanted the job for two reasons. First, she wants to save money for a language course in Turkey next summer. Second, her parents said that she should learn the value of money. At first, she thought the work would be boring, but she was surprised by how much she liked it.

The owner of the shop is Mr Nazarov, an old man with white hair who has sold books for forty years. On her first day, he taught her how to arrange the shelves by subject and how to find any book in less than a minute. He also gave her one rule: never tell a customer that you do not know the answer. Instead, say that you will find out.

Her duties are simple. She opens the shop at nine, cleans the tables, helps the customers and works at the cash desk.

The job is not always easy. In May, she had an important exam at school and she was also working on Saturdays. She was so tired that she made a mistake at the cash desk and gave a customer too much change. Mr Nazarov was not angry. He told her to take the next Saturday off and study. She passed her exam with a good mark and came back the following week.

Now Sevara has saved almost four hundred thousand soums. She still needs about as much again before she can pay for the course. She thinks she will reach her goal by April. When she finishes school, she may study literature, and she would love to open her own bookshop one day.

items.prompt: Where did Bahrom work before he became a taxi driver?
items.passage:
Bahrom has driven a taxi in Tashkent for nine years. Before that, he worked in a shoe factory, but the factory closed and he needed a new job quickly. His brother lent him some money, and Bahrom bought a small white car. He still drives the same car today, although it is getting old.

He usually works from two in the afternoon until midnight, because most people need a taxi in the evening. The best time is Friday night, when the streets are full of people who go to restaurants and weddings. The worst time is early morning, when almost nobody is outside and the money is very small.

Bahrom says that he has met every kind of person. Once a famous singer sat in his back seat and sang quietly all the way to the airport. Another time a tourist from Spain did not speak any Russian or Uzbek, so they used a phone to translate. After twenty minutes, the tourist was laughing and Bahrom had learned four Spanish words.

The job also has bad sides. The roads are often crowded, and he sits for ten hours a day, so his back hurts. He spends about a third of his income on petrol and repairs. Last winter his engine broke down in the middle of the night, and he had to push the car for two hundred metres in the snow.

Still, he has a few rules that make the work better. He always keeps the car clean, he never drives fast and he gives every child a small sweet. "Clients remember small things," he says. "That is why many of them call me directly instead of using an app."

Now Bahrom is learning English with an app on his phone. He studies for half an hour before work, because more tourists come to the city every year. He hopes that in two years he will be able to talk with foreign passengers without a translator.

Bahrom has driven a taxi in Tashkent for nine years. Before that, he worked in a shoe factory, but the factory closed and he needed a new job quickly. His brother lent him some money, and Bahrom bought a small white car. He still drives the same car today, although it is getting old.

He usually works from two in the afternoon until midnight, because most people need a taxi in the evening. The best time is Friday night, when the streets are full of people who go to restaurants and weddings. The worst time is early morning, when almost nobody is outside and the money is very small.

Bahrom says that he has met every kind of person. Once a famous singer sat in his back seat and sang quietly all the way to the airport. Another time a tourist from Spain did not speak any Russian or Uzbek, so they used a phone to translate. After twenty minutes, the tourist was laughing and Bahrom had learned four Spanish words.

The job also has bad sides. The roads are often crowded, and he sits for ten hours a day, so his back hurts. He spends about a third of his income on petrol and repairs. Last winter his engine broke down in the middle of the night, and he had to push the car for two hundred metres in the snow.

Still, he has a few rules that make the work better. He always keeps the car clean, he never drives fast and he gives every child a small sweet. "Clients remember small things," he says. "That is why many of them call me directly instead of using an app."

Now Bahrom is learning English with an app on his phone. He studies for half an hour before work, because more tourists come to the city every year. He hopes that in two years he will be able to talk with foreign passengers without a translator.

items.prompt: When does Nigora's night shift last?
items.answer: from eight in the evening to eight in the morning
items.passage:
Dr Nigora Yusupova is a young doctor in a city hospital in Andijan. Twice a week she works the night shift, from eight in the evening to eight in the morning. She says that nights in hospital are completely different from days. The corridors are quiet, the lights are low, and every sound seems louder.

Last Thursday began calmly. At nine o'clock she checked the patients on the second floor. There were twenty-two of them, and most were asleep. She spoke for a few minutes with an old man called Mr Salimov, who could not sleep because he was worried about his operation. She explained everything slowly, and he finally closed his eyes.

At midnight, the telephone rang. An ambulance was bringing a boy of ten who had fallen from a tree and hurt his arm. Nigora and two nurses prepared the emergency room. The boy arrived in eleven minutes, crying and very frightened. She took an X-ray, which showed a small break in the bone. Then she put on a plaster, and she gave him a toy rabbit from a special box that she keeps for children.

After that, she had a short rest in the doctors' room. At three o'clock, a woman with a very high temperature arrived, and Nigora stayed with her for almost an hour until the medicine began to work.

The hardest moment of the night came at five o'clock. A car accident brought three injured people at once. Nigora was the only doctor in the emergency room, so she called a colleague from home. He came in twenty minutes, and together they helped everyone. Luckily, none of the injuries was very serious.

At eight o'clock, the morning doctors arrived. Nigora wrote her notes and walked slowly to the door. She was exhausted, but she smiled when she remembered the little boy. "This is why I chose this job," she said. At home she slept until three in the afternoon.
options: from eight in the evening to eight in the morning

items.prompt: How long has Jamshid been a builder?
items.passage:
Jamshid is a builder, and he has been building houses in Karshi for fifteen years. Last year his team built a two-storey house for a family with four children. The work took seven months, and Jamshid says it was one of his favourite projects.

The team has six people. There are two bricklayers, an electrician, a plumber, a painter and Jamshid himself, who is the leader. They start at seven in the morning because it is cooler, and they finish at four. In summer the temperature on the roof can reach forty-five degrees, so everyone drinks a lot of water and wears a hat.

First, they dug the ground and made the base of the house from concrete. This step is the most important one, Jamshid explains, because a house with a bad base will not last. Then the bricklayers built the walls. They put around eleven thousand bricks, and they worked so fast that the first floor was finished in six weeks.

In the middle of the project, there was a serious problem. A storm came in October, and strong wind broke the temporary roof. Water went into the rooms and made the new walls wet. The team worked on Saturday and Sunday to repair the damage. The family was very grateful, and the father brought them a big pot of plov every day for a week.

Safety is very important on a building site. Every worker must wear a helmet and strong boots, and nobody is allowed to climb a ladder alone. Jamshid once saw a man fall from the second floor because he was not careful. Fortunately, the man only broke his leg, but since then Jamshid checks all the equipment every morning.

When the house was ready, the family invited the team to a small party. The youngest child, a girl called Ruxsora, drew a picture of the house and gave it to Jamshid. Now he is planning a bigger project: a small school for a village near the city.

items.prompt: How old was Timur at the interview?
items.passage:
Timur was twenty-six when he went to the most important interview of his life. A large travel company in Tashkent wanted a new assistant manager, and the salary was twice as big as his salary at that time. He prepared for a week.

On the morning of the interview, however, everything went wrong. His alarm clock did not ring because the battery was dead, so he woke up at eight fifteen. The interview was at nine, and the office was across the city. He ran to the metro, but the train was delayed for ten minutes. When he finally arrived, he was twelve minutes late and his shirt was wet from the rain.

The manager, Mrs Ergasheva, looked at her watch and said nothing. Timur apologised, but he made a second mistake: he told her that the metro was always late in Tashkent, as if it was her problem. Then she asked him why he wanted to work there, and he forgot all his careful answers. He said that he wanted the job because the salary was good. The room became very quiet.

Timur understood that the interview was going badly, so he took a deep breath and told the truth. He said that he was nervous, that he had really wanted this job for two years and that he was sorry for being late. Mrs Ergasheva smiled a little for the first time. She told him that honesty was something she liked in people.

He did not get the job. A week later, the company sent him an email with a polite refusal. But Mrs Ergasheva also called him personally and said that another position, a sales role, would open in March, and she would remember him.

Timur learned three lessons. First, always set two alarms. Second, leave home one hour earlier than you think. Third, never complain about small problems in an interview. In March he applied for the sales position and, this time, he arrived fifteen minutes early.

items.prompt: How long ago did Gulbahor start working at the supermarket?
items.passage:
Gulbahor started working at a large supermarket in Samarkand six years ago. She began as a cashier, and her first salary was very small. In the beginning, she planned to stay only for a year, but she kept learning new things and the job became more interesting.

In her second year, she noticed that the queues at the cash desks were often long on Saturdays. She had an idea: open two more cash desks between eleven and two, the busiest hours, and move the new workers there from the storeroom. She wrote a short report and gave it to her manager, Mr Tursunov. He tried her idea for one month. The queues became thirty per cent shorter, and customers wrote nice comments on the shop's website.

After that, people began to trust her. When a new cashier started, the manager asked Gulbahor to teach her. She trained fourteen new employees in four years, and she always stayed patient even when they made many mistakes. She also took an evening course in management, which took eight months.

Last month, Mr Tursunov called her into his office. She thought she had done something wrong, and her heart was beating fast. Instead, he told her that the company wanted to promote her to the position of shift supervisor. She would lead a team of twenty people, and her salary would rise by forty per cent. She was so surprised that she could not speak, and then she asked for one day to think. He laughed and agreed.

items.prompt: How many students visited the factory?
items.passage:
Last Tuesday, our class of twenty-four students visited a furniture factory near Namangan. Our teacher, Mrs Rahimova, organised the trip because we are studying different jobs in our English lessons. We left school at eight o'clock in a small yellow bus, and the journey took forty minutes.

At the gate, a guide named Mr Abdullayev gave us helmets and yellow jackets. He explained that safety is the first rule in the factory, so we must stay together and never touch the machines. Then we entered a huge hall that smelled of fresh wood. The noise was so loud that we could hardly hear him, and he had to shout.

First, we saw the place where the wood arrives. Big trucks bring trees from forests in the north, and large machines cut them into long, flat boards. After that, the boards go to the second hall, where workers measure, cut and join them. I was surprised that many machines are controlled by computers, but there are still people who sand the surfaces by hand. One of them, an old man named Mr Hakimov, said that he had done this work for thirty-one years and that a machine could never feel the wood as he did.

The factory makes about two hundred chairs and eighty tables every day. Some of them are sold in Uzbekistan, and the others go to Kazakhstan and Turkey. In the last room, we watched workers paint and pack the furniture. A girl in my class, Zarina, asked how much a table cost, and the guide said that the cheapest one was ninety dollars.

At noon we ate lunch in the factory canteen. A young woman told us that she had studied design and now she draws new models for chairs.

On the way back, everybody was tired but happy. Mrs Rahimova asked us to write a short report about the visit, and I am going to write about Mr Hakimov, because his story was my favourite.

Last Tuesday, our class of twenty-four students visited a furniture factory near Namangan. Our teacher, Mrs Rahimova, organised the trip because we are studying different jobs in our English lessons. We left school at eight o'clock in a small yellow bus, and the journey took forty minutes.

Then we entered a huge hall that smelled of fresh wood. The noise was so loud that we could hardly hear him, and he had to shout.

First, we saw the place where the wood arrives. Big trucks bring trees from forests in the north, and large machines cut them into long, flat boards. After that, the boards go to the second hall, where workers measure, cut and join them. I was surprised that many machines are controlled by computers, but there are still people who sand the surfaces by hand. items.prompt: For how long has Lola worked from home?
items.passage:
Lola is a graphic designer, and for the past two years she has worked from home. Before that, she had an office job in the centre of Tashkent. Every day she spent almost two hours in traffic, and she was always tired when she arrived. When her company decided to let employees work at home three days a week, she was delighted.

She lives in a small flat with her husband, Sanjar, and their dog, Max. In the beginning, she worked at the kitchen table, but her back began to hurt. So she bought a proper desk and a comfortable chair, and she put them in the corner of the bedroom next to the window. "A good place for work is very important," she says.

Working from home has several advantages. First, Lola saves two hours every day, and she uses that time to go for a walk or to cook a healthy breakfast. Second, she can concentrate better because the flat is quiet. She also saves money, because she does not buy lunch in cafes or pay for the bus.

But there are some problems, too. The first month was hard because she did not have a clear schedule. She often worked until midnight, and then she could not sleep. Another problem is loneliness. She misses talking with her colleagues about small things like films or the weather. Now she has a rule: she starts at nine, takes a break at one and stops at six. She also phones a colleague every Wednesday just to chat.

Her company has a video meeting every Monday morning. Last week, Max jumped on the desk during the meeting and everyone laughed.

On the two days when she goes to the office, Lola enjoys meeting her friends and having lunch with them. She thinks the best system is a mix of home and office. "If I worked at home five days a week, I would probably go crazy," she says. "But three days is perfect."

items.prompt: How many calls does Farhod answer every day?
items.passage:
Farhod works in a call centre for a mobile phone company in Tashkent. He answers about ninety calls every day, and he has been in this job for eighteen months. When he began, he thought it would be easy: pick up the phone, listen and give an answer. Soon he understood it was much more difficult.

The call centre is a big room with sixty desks, and the work is done in shifts. Farhod's shift begins at seven in the morning and ends at three. Every worker wears a headset and sits in front of two screens. On the first screen, there is information about the customer. On the second one, there is a list of common problems and their solutions. The company wants the average call to be shorter than six minutes.

Most customers are polite, but some are angry. Last week a man called three times in one hour because his internet was not working. By the third call he was shouting. Farhod stayed calm, apologised and sent an engineer to the man's house. The next day, the man called again to say thank you, which made Farhod's whole week.

The most important skill, says Farhod, is listening. His supervisor, Ms Lee, teaches the team to repeat the problem in their own words before offering help. This technique has reduced the number of mistakes by a quarter.

The job is tiring, because workers sit for eight hours and talk almost without a break. They have only a thirty-minute lunch and two short breaks of ten minutes. Many employees leave after one year. Farhod stays because he has made good friends and because the company pays for English lessons. Last month he passed an exam and now he can answer calls from foreign customers.

In the future, Farhod would like to become a team leader. He says he will need to learn more about computers first, so he is going to start an online course in October.

items.prompt: How many years did Mr Ismoilov work as a teacher?
items.passage:
After thirty-eight years as a mathematics teacher, Mr Ismoilov retired last June. He is sixty-two years old, and he worked in the same school in Khiva since he was twenty-four. On his last day, the students gave him a cake, a big card with three hundred signatures and a photograph of all his classes. He said that he did not cry, but his wife, Halima, says that she saw him wipe his eyes twice.

The first weeks of retirement were strange. He woke up at six o'clock out of habit and then did not know what to do. His wife told him that he should find a hobby, or he would become bored and difficult to live with.

So he made a list. First, he wanted to repair the old bicycles in the garage. Second, he wanted to learn to play the dutar, a traditional instrument that his father once played. Third, he wanted to travel. He had never left Uzbekistan, and now he dreams of seeing the sea in Turkey.

Three months later, he has already finished the first two things. He repaired four bicycles and gave them to children in his street. He also takes dutar lessons twice a week from a young teacher called Aziza. She says that he practises more than any of her other students, probably because he knows from his own teaching how important practice is.

There was one surprise. In September, the director of his old school called him and asked if he could help weak students with mathematics on Saturday mornings, without pay. At first he hesitated, then said yes. Now eight children come to his house every Saturday, and Halima makes tea and biscuits for them.

Mr Ismoilov says that retirement is not the end of work; it is a different kind of work. He is saving money for his trip, and next spring he and Halima are going to fly to Istanbul for ten days.

items.prompt: Where was Jasur playing football when he fell?
items.answer: In the yard behind his school
items.passage:
Last winter, Jasur, a twelve-year-old boy from Samarkand, broke his arm. It happened on a Saturday morning in January. He was playing football with his friends in the yard behind his school when he slipped on some ice. He fell on his left arm and felt a terrible pain. His friend Bobur ran to call Jasur's father, who worked at a shop nearby.

Jasur's father drove him to the city hospital. They waited for forty minutes because many people were there. At last a young doctor called Dr. Karimova took Jasur to a small room. She looked at his arm carefully and asked if he could move his fingers. Jasur could move them, but it hurt a lot. Then a nurse took him for an X-ray. The picture showed a small break in the bone, just above the wrist.

Dr. Karimova explained that the arm was not in a bad condition. She said he was lucky because the bone would heal well. He needed a cast for six weeks. Jasur chose a blue cast because blue is his favourite colour. The doctor told him not to play sports and not to carry heavy bags. She also said he should eat more milk, cheese and eggs because they help bones to become strong again.

The first week was difficult. Jasur couldn't write with his left hand, so his sister Malika helped him with his homework. He also couldn't ride his bicycle, which made him sad. However, his classmates all signed his cast and drew funny pictures on it.

After six weeks Jasur went back to the hospital. The doctor took off the cast, and his arm looked thin and pale. She gave him some easy exercises to do every evening. Two weeks later he was playing football again, but now he is much more careful on icy days and always wears warm shoes with good soles.
options: In the yard behind his school

items.prompt: When did Dilnoza's flu begin?
items.passage:
Dilnoza usually feels healthy, but last November she had the flu for a whole week. It began on Monday morning. She woke up with a sore throat and a headache, and her body felt very hot. Her mother, Gulnora, took her temperature. It was thirty-eight degrees, so Dilnoza stayed at home and didn't go to school.

On Tuesday a doctor came to the house. He listened to Dilnoza's chest and looked at her throat. He said it was not a dangerous illness, but she needed to rest. He told her to drink a lot of water and warm tea with honey and lemon. He also gave her some medicine to take twice a day, after breakfast and before bed. Dilnoza didn't like the taste, but she took it every time.

Wednesday was the worst day. Dilnoza had a bad cough and she couldn't sleep at night. Her nose was red and her eyes were wet. Her mother made a big pot of chicken soup with carrots and rice, and Dilnoza ate a little of it for lunch. She spent most of the day in bed with a blanket, watching old films on her tablet and reading her favourite magazine.

On Thursday she began to feel better. Her temperature went down to thirty-seven degrees, and she was hungry again. She sat by the window for an hour and watched the snow. Her best friend Zarina sent her a funny message and a photo of the class, which made her smile.

Unfortunately, on Friday her little brother Anvar caught the flu too. Now Gulnora had two sick children at home! By Sunday, Dilnoza felt strong again. She went back to school the next Monday. Her teacher told her to wash her hands often, and she promised that next winter she would eat more fruit and wear a warmer scarf.

items.prompt: How long is a marathon in the text?
items.passage:
Alisher is twenty-nine and works in a bank in Tashkent. Two years ago he couldn't run for ten minutes without stopping. Last April he finished his first marathon, which is forty-two kilometres long. This is the story of his training.

It all started in October, when his cousin Bahrom said, "Let's run the spring marathon together." Alisher laughed, but he agreed. On the first day he ran only three kilometres, and he was very tired afterwards. He was not discouraged. He made a plan and ran three times a week: two short runs on weekdays and one long run on Sunday. Every two weeks he added one more kilometre to his long run.

In March, he bought a new pair of running shoes. Before that he was training in old shoes, and he got a painful blister on his foot. The shop assistant told him that good shoes are the most important thing for a runner. Alisher also started to eat more pasta, rice and bananas, and he drank a lot of water.

The race day was sunny and not too hot. More than two thousand people were at the start line at seven o'clock. There were water stations every five kilometres, and children were giving out orange slices. Alisher felt great for the first twenty kilometres. At the thirty-kilometre mark, however, his legs were very heavy, and he nearly stopped. Bahrom ran beside him and talked about food and holidays, and that helped a lot.

Alisher finished in four hours and twenty minutes. His mother was waiting at the finish line with a bunch of flowers. He couldn't walk well for two days, but he was extremely happy. Now he wants to run a faster marathon next year, and he will start training in the autumn again.

items.prompt: When did Nilufar's toothache begin?
items.passage:
Nilufar is ten years old, and she was afraid of dentists. Last month, however, she had a bad toothache and she had to go to one. It began on Friday night. She was eating a piece of chocolate when a sharp pain went through her tooth. She couldn't sleep well, and in the morning she told her father about it.

Her father called the dental clinic near their house and made an appointment for ten o'clock. In the car Nilufar's hands were cold and she didn't say a word. At the clinic a friendly dentist called Dr. Ahmedov met them. He had a kind voice and a funny blue hat with pictures of animals. He asked Nilufar to sit in a big chair and open her mouth.

Dr. Ahmedov looked at her teeth with a small mirror. "You have a hole in one tooth at the back," he said. "It is because you eat too many sweet things." Nilufar felt a little ashamed. The dentist said that he would clean the tooth and put in a filling. First he gave her an injection, so she wouldn't feel any pain. Nilufar closed her eyes tightly, but she only felt a small push.

The visit took thirty minutes. Dr. Ahmedov gave her headphones with music, and that helped her to stay calm. When he finished, he showed her the mirror and said she was very brave. She got a sticker of a smiling tiger and a new green toothbrush.

Before they left, Dr. Ahmedov gave her some advice. She should brush her teeth twice a day for two minutes, and she should eat fewer sweets. He told her to come back in six months for a check-up. In the car, Nilufar said, "That wasn't so terrible! Next time I won't be afraid."

items.prompt: What did Sardor eat for breakfast before?
items.passage:
My name is Sardor, and I am fifteen. Until last autumn I never ate a good breakfast. Every morning I drank sweet black tea and ate two pieces of white bread with jam. I was always in a hurry, and I thought breakfast wasn't important. However, by ten o'clock I was usually tired, hungry and unable to think in my maths lesson.

One day my teacher, Mrs. Hughes, noticed that I was falling asleep in class. She asked me what I had eaten that morning. When I told her, she laughed kindly and said, "Your body needs better fuel, Sardor." She explained that a healthy breakfast gives you energy for the whole morning. She told me to eat more protein and fibre, and less sugar.

I decided to try. First, I woke up fifteen minutes earlier. Now I make porridge with milk, and I add chopped apples and a handful of walnuts. Sometimes I have a boiled egg too. I drink green tea or a glass of water instead of sweet black tea. My mother was surprised at first, but she quite likes the new menu, and she often eats porridge with me.

The change wasn't easy in the first week. I missed my jam and white bread, and I even bought a chocolate bar at school on Wednesday. But after two weeks I noticed something important. I wasn't tired in the middle of the morning anymore, and I could concentrate better. My marks in maths went up from a C to a B.

On weekends I give myself a treat and make pancakes with honey. My little sister Zarina still prefers chocolate cereal with cold milk, but I hope she will change her mind soon. A good breakfast is cheaper than you think. Mine costs about the same as my old one, and it makes me feel much stronger.

I was always in a hurry, and I thought breakfast wasn't important. However, by ten o'clock I was usually tired, hungry and unable to think in my maths lesson.

One day my teacher, Mrs. Hughes, noticed that I was falling asleep in class. She asked me what I had eaten that morning. When I told her, she laughed kindly and said, "Your body needs better fuel, Sardor." She explained that a healthy breakfast gives you energy for the whole morning. She told me to eat more protein and fibre, and less sugar.

I decided to try. First, I woke up fifteen minutes earlier. Now I make porridge with milk, and I add chopped apples and a handful of walnuts. Sometimes I have a boiled egg too. I drink green tea or a glass of water instead of sweet black tea. My mother was surprised at first, but she quite likes the new menu, and she often eats porridge with me.

The change wasn't easy in the first week. I missed my jam and white bread, and I even bought a chocolate bar at school on Wednesday. But after two weeks I noticed something important. I wasn't tired in the middle of the morning anymore, and I could concentrate better. My marks in maths went up from a C to a B.

On weekends I give myself a treat and make pancakes with honey. My little sister Zarina still prefers chocolate cereal with cold milk, but I hope she will change her mind soon. A good breakfast is cheaper than you think. Mine costs about the same as my old one, and it makes me feel much stronger.

items.prompt: Which race did Emma swim?
items.passage:
Emma is fourteen and lives in Leeds, in the north of England. She has been a swimmer since she was seven years old. Last Saturday she took part in the county championship, the biggest race of her life. She swam the hundred metres freestyle.

Her alarm clock rang at half past six. Emma wasn't hungry because she was very nervous, but her mother made her eat a banana and some toast. They drove to the swimming pool, which was forty minutes from their home. The building was big and noisy, and there were hundreds of people on the benches. Emma's coach, Mr. Collins, was waiting for her near the entrance. He told her to relax and think about her technique, not about the other girls.

Emma trained five times a week at the pool, and twice she got up at five thirty to swim before school. She sometimes felt tired and wanted to stop, but her friend Priya always encouraged her. Priya was in the crowd on Saturday with a big sign that said "Go, Emma!"

In the final, Emma was in lane four. When the whistle blew, she jumped into the water, but her start wasn't good. At the first turn she was third. She was behind a tall girl from Manchester called Hannah and a girl from York. Emma remembered her coach's words and kept her stroke long and smooth. At seventy-five metres she was second. In the last fifteen metres she swam faster than ever and touched the wall just before Hannah.

Emma won by only two tenths of a second. Her time was fifty-nine seconds, which was her best ever. She received a gold medal and a small cup. "I couldn't believe it," she said afterwards. That evening the family celebrated with fish and chips, and Emma slept for ten hours.

items.prompt: How many hours did Bekzod sleep before his problem was solved?
items.passage:
Bekzod is a nineteen-year-old university student in Bukhara. For three months he had a serious problem: he couldn't sleep well. He usually went to bed after two o'clock in the morning and woke up at seven. That meant he slept only five hours a night. During the day he felt tired and bad-tempered, and he forgot things easily.

There were several reasons for his problem. First, he was studying for important exams, so he stayed up late with his books. Second, he drank three or four cups of strong coffee every day, even in the evening. Third, he lay in bed and played games on his phone until his eyes hurt. Sometimes he fell asleep with the phone in his hand.

One morning, Bekzod nearly fell asleep during an exam. His friend Otabek was worried and told him to see the university nurse. Her name was Mrs. Rakhimova, and she was very kind. She asked many questions and listened carefully. Then she gave him four simple rules.

The first rule was to go to bed at ten o'clock and get up at six every day, even at weekends. The second rule was no coffee after four o'clock in the afternoon. The third was to turn off the phone one hour before bed and to read a paper book or listen to quiet music instead. The last rule was to keep his bedroom dark, cool and quiet.

At first it was hard. During the first three nights Bekzod lay awake for a long time. But after ten days he began to fall asleep quickly, and he now sleeps about eight hours. He feels more cheerful, and he can remember his lessons much better. His exam results were also better than he expected. He says that good sleep is more useful than extra study hours at night.

items.prompt: Why did Madina decide to join a gym?
items.answer: Her doctor said she needed to move more
items.passage:
Madina is twenty-eight and works in an office in Tashkent. For a long time she sat at her desk for nine hours a day, and in the evenings she went home and watched television. In the summer she noticed that she was always tired and that her back hurt. Her doctor said she needed to move more. So in September she decided to join a gym.

The gym was near her office, only fifteen minutes on foot. The monthly price was two hundred thousand som, which Madina thought was fair. On the first day a trainer called Rustam showed her all the machines. He gave her a simple plan: three visits a week, on Monday, Wednesday and Friday at six o'clock in the evening, and one hour each time. The first twenty minutes were for running on a machine, and the rest for light weights.

The first month was hard. After the first visit, Madina's legs hurt so much that she could hardly climb the stairs at home. She almost gave up in the second week. However, she bought a small notebook and wrote down every visit with a tick. Seeing the ticks gave her a feeling of success. Her friend Lola joined her in October, and they trained together and laughed a lot.

After three months, Madina noticed big changes. She lost five kilograms, and her back didn't hurt any more. She slept better and had more energy at work. She also began to take the stairs instead of the lift and to walk in the park at weekends.

Now the gym is a normal part of her week, like brushing her teeth. Rustam says that the secret is not to train very hard, but to train regularly. Madina agrees. She says it is easier to keep a habit when you have a friend, a plan and a notebook.
options: Her doctor said she needed to move more

items.prompt: Whom did Kamol's team play against in May?
items.passage:
Kamol is seventeen, and football is his whole life. He plays for the youth team of his town in Namangan, and he is the best striker in the team. Last May his team played an important match against a team from Andijan. Kamol had already scored one goal when the accident happened.

It was the seventieth minute, and the score was one all. Kamol received a long pass and ran towards the goal. Suddenly a defender tackled him from the side. Kamol's foot stayed on the ground, but his knee turned in a strange way. He heard a loud click and fell down in great pain. The referee stopped the game, and two men carried him off the pitch.

An ambulance took Kamol to hospital, where a doctor examined his knee and arranged an examination with a special machine. The result was bad news: one of the ligaments in his knee was badly damaged. The doctor said he couldn't play football for eight weeks, and he must rest his leg and use crutches. Kamol was very upset. He cried that night because the big tournament was in July.

The next day his coach, Mr. Yusupov, visited him and brought some fruit. He said, "Don't worry. Your job now is to get better." He also asked Kamol to help him as an assistant at training sessions. Kamol watched his teammates from a bench and gave them advice. Three times a week, he also visited a physiotherapist, Ms. Karimova, who taught him exercises to make his knee strong again.

After nine weeks, Kamol was ready to run again. At first he played only for twenty minutes in friendly matches. In July he joined the tournament as a substitute and scored in the final. "I will never play carelessly again," he said. His team won the cup.

items.prompt: How many nights did Peter spend in hospital?
items.passage:
Last spring I spent three nights in hospital. I am Peter, I am sixteen, and I live in a small town near Manchester. It began on a Sunday afternoon with a strange pain in my stomach. At first I thought I had eaten something bad, but the pain got worse every hour. By the evening I couldn't stand up straight, and my mother drove me to the hospital.

A doctor examined me and said I had appendicitis. I needed an operation immediately. I was frightened, but a nurse called Sophie held my hand and told me everything was going to be fine. The operation took place on Monday morning at nine o'clock. I remember counting to ten when the anaesthetic began to work, and then I fell asleep.

When I woke up, I was in a ward with three other boys. The room had four beds, a big window and a small television. My stomach hurt, but the pain was not terrible. My mother and father were sitting next to my bed. Dad had brought some magazines and my favourite chocolate, but the nurse said I couldn't eat solid food until the next day. I only had soup and water.

The days in hospital were long. In the next bed, there was a boy called Ravi who was ten and played cards all day. He taught me a new game, and we played for hours. The hospital food was better than I expected, especially the pasta on Tuesday. Every morning a doctor came and checked my wound.

On Wednesday afternoon the doctor said I could go home. I was glad but also a little sad to say goodbye to Sophie and Ravi. I had to stay away from sports for a month, and I stayed at home for two weeks. Now I feel completely well, and I have a small scar on my stomach to remember the adventure.
