items.prompt: Why did Sevara decide to lose weight?
items.answer: She wanted to fit into a dress for her sister's wedding
items.passage:
Sevara is twenty-four, and she lives in Fergana. Last winter her older sister Gulchehra announced that she would get married in June. Sevara was very happy, but there was a small problem. She wanted to fit into a beautiful blue dress that she had bought two years before, and it was too tight. She decided to lose some weight before the wedding.

In March she visited a dietitian, Dr. Olimov. He asked her about her habits. Sevara admitted that she drank two or three bottles of sweet lemonade every day, ate a lot of bread, and had big dinners late at night. Dr. Olimov didn't give her a strict, boring diet. Instead he made a simple plan with five rules.

First, no sugary drinks, only water and unsweetened tea. Second, vegetables at lunch and dinner, filling half of her plate. Third, smaller portions and no food after eight o'clock in the evening. Fourth, a walk of thirty minutes every day. Fifth, one small treat on Sunday, because he said a plan with no pleasure usually fails.

The first two weeks were the hardest. Sevara had headaches and often dreamed about cakes. But she didn't give up. She cooked soups and salads, and she found tasty recipes on the internet. Her mother supported her and stopped buying lemonade. Every Sunday Sevara ate a piece of her favourite chocolate cake and felt happy, not guilty.

By June she had lost six kilograms. The blue dress fitted perfectly! At the wedding, many relatives asked her about her secret. "It wasn't magic," she said. "I simply ate better, moved more and was patient." She is now going to keep these habits, because she feels lighter and healthier than before.

items.prompt: When did the wedding take place?
items.passage:
Sevara is twenty-four, and she lives in Fergana. Last winter her older sister Gulchehra announced that she would get married in June. Sevara was very happy, but there was a small problem. She wanted to fit into a beautiful blue dress that she had bought two years before, and it was too tight. She decided to lose some weight before the wedding.

In March she visited a dietitian, Dr. Olimov. He asked her about her habits. Sevara admitted that she drank two or three bottles of sweet lemonade every day, ate a lot of bread, and had big dinners late at night. Dr. Olimov didn't give her a strict, boring diet. Instead he made a simple plan with five rules.

First, no sugary drinks, only water and unsweetened tea. Second, vegetables at lunch and dinner, filling half of her plate. Third, smaller portions and no food after eight o'clock in the evening. Fourth, a walk of thirty minutes every day. Fifth, one small treat on Sunday, because he said a plan with no pleasure usually fails.

The first two weeks were the hardest. Sevara had headaches and often dreamed about cakes. But she didn't give up. She cooked soups and salads, and she found tasty recipes on the internet. Her mother supported her and stopped buying lemonade. Every Sunday Sevara ate a piece of her favourite chocolate cake and felt happy, not guilty.

By June she had lost six kilograms. The blue dress fitted perfectly! At the wedding, many relatives asked her about her secret. "It wasn't magic," she said. "I simply ate better, moved more and was patient." She is now going to keep these habits, because she feels lighter and healthier than before.

items.prompt: Who gave Daniel the lesson as a present?
items.passage:
Daniel is a shy fifteen-year-old boy from Madrid. Last month his uncle gave him a surprise present: a first lesson at a boxing club near their home. Daniel wasn't sure about it. He thought boxing was only about fighting, and he didn't like violence. But his uncle explained that modern boxing is mostly a fitness sport and teaches you discipline. So on Thursday evening Daniel walked to the club with his sports bag and some doubts.

The club was a big room with two rings, a lot of heavy bags and mirrors on the wall. It smelled of sweat and leather. The coach, a short strong man named Azamat, was originally from Uzbekistan. He greeted Daniel with a warm smile and a firm handshake. "Today we learn the basics," he said. "Nobody will hit you."

They began with a warm-up. Daniel skipped with a rope for ten minutes, which was much harder than it looked. Then he did some stretching and a few push-ups. After that Azamat showed him the correct stance: feet apart, knees slightly bent, hands near the chin. Daniel practised the jab, a quick straight punch, on a heavy bag. At first his punches were slow and weak, but after twenty minutes they were faster and stronger.

At the end of the lesson Daniel was exhausted. His arms were shaking, and his T-shirt was wet. Yet he felt wonderful. Azamat told him that he had a good rhythm and learned quickly. "Come on Tuesday and Thursday," he said. "After three months, you'll be a different person."

The next morning Daniel's shoulders hurt, but he was smiling. He told his uncle that boxing was harder than football, and much more interesting. He has paid for the whole month, and in a year he hopes to take part in a small club competition.

Last August four friends decided to climb a mountain near Tashkent, in the Chimgan range. The group included Temur, a sports teacher, his wife Lola, their friend Sarah from Canada, and a guide named Farhod. It was Sarah's first time in the mountains, so everybody was excited, and a little worried.

They met at half past four in the morning and drove to the starting point in a small bus. They began walking at five o'clock, while the sky was still dark. Each person carried a rucksack with two litres of water, bread, cheese, apples, nuts and a warm jacket. Farhod told them to walk slowly and steadily and not to talk too much, in order to save energy.

The first two hours were easy. The path went through green forest, and they heard birds and a small river. Then the trees ended, and the path became steeper and rocky. At about nine o'clock they stopped for breakfast on a large flat stone. Sarah took many photos of the valley, which looked like a green carpet below them.

The last part was the hardest. The air was thinner and colder, and Sarah had a headache. Farhod made her drink water and rest for ten minutes. Near the top there was some snow, even in summer. They reached the summit at eleven o'clock after six hours of walking. It was three thousand three hundred metres above the sea. Everyone was tired but proud. They saw an eagle flying over the peaks, and they could see the whole city far away like a map.

The way down took four hours, and their knees hurt. They arrived at the bus at about three in the afternoon. That evening Sarah said it was the most beautiful day of her trip and that she would come back next year to climb a higher mountain.

items.prompt: Where does Katya come from?
items.passage:
Every June, the sports club in our town organises a tennis tournament for young players. This year, the final was between two sixteen-year-old girls: Sofia from Tashkent and Katya from Samarkand. They had played against each other many times, and they were also good friends. Both of them wanted the silver cup very much.

The match started at ten o'clock on Sunday morning. About two hundred people were sitting around the court, and the weather was warm and sunny. Katya was taller and she had a powerful serve. In the first set she played very well and won six games to three. Sofia made many mistakes because she was nervous. Her coach, Mr. Brown, told her during the break, "Be calm. Make her run more."

In the second set Sofia changed her tactics. She hit the ball softly and to different corners of the court, and Katya had to run a lot. The set was very close. At five games all, it began to rain, and the referee stopped the match for thirty minutes. Players and fans waited under umbrellas. Sofia drank some juice and ate a banana. When they came back, she had more energy. She won the set seven games to five.

The third set was the most exciting. Katya led by four games to two, and everybody thought she would win. But Sofia refused to give up. She won four games in a row and finished the match with a beautiful serve. The final score was six games to four.

The crowd stood up and applauded. At the net the girls hugged each other. Sofia received the silver cup and a bunch of flowers. "Katya is a great player," she said in her speech. "I only won because I was a bit more patient today." Next year Katya will try to take revenge.

items.prompt: When did Oybek's symptoms begin every year?
items.passage:
Oybek is twelve years old, and every spring he used to have the same problem. When the trees began to bloom in April, his nose started to run, his eyes became red and itchy, and he sneezed twenty or thirty times a day. His mother thought that he had a long cold. His teacher thought he wasn't sleeping enough. In fact, Oybek had an allergy.

Last year his aunt, who is a nurse, noticed that the symptoms appeared only in spring and in the evenings when Oybek played with their cat, Murka. She took him to an allergy specialist, Dr. Nazarova. The doctor did a skin test. She put small drops on his arm and waited twenty minutes. Several red spots appeared. The test showed that Oybek was allergic to pollen from trees and grass and also to cat hair.

Dr. Nazarova explained that an allergy happens when the body reacts too strongly to something harmless. She gave Oybek some tablets to take every morning during spring, and she also gave him a list of useful rules. He should keep the windows of his bedroom closed on windy days, wash his hair and change his clothes after playing outside, and not do sport in the park in the morning when there is a lot of pollen in the air.

The cat was a sad question. Oybek loved Murka very much, but the doctor said it was better for his health to live without her. In the end, his aunt took Murka to her own house, which is only five minutes away, so Oybek can still visit her for short times and wash his hands afterwards.

This spring was much better. Oybek sneezed only a few times and his eyes were fine. He could play football with his friends without feeling ill. "I'm happy that I finally know the reason," he says. "Now I can enjoy flowers from a distance!"

items.prompt: How old was Dilnoza's old computer?
items.passage:
Dilnoza had wanted a new laptop for a long time. Her old computer was five years old, and it was very slow. Last month it stopped working in the middle of her English homework, and she lost two hours of work. That was the last straw. She decided to buy a better one before the new term started.

First, she asked her cousin Rustam for advice. Rustam works in a computer shop in Tashkent. He told her, "You should not buy the most expensive laptop. You need a light one with a good battery, because you will carry it to university every day." Dilnoza agreed. She saved money for three months and finally had nine million som.

On Saturday morning she went to the shop with Rustam. There were many models on the shelves, and she was a little confused. The first laptop was cheaper than the others, but it was heavy and the screen was small. The second one was lighter and had a bigger screen, but it cost eleven million som. The third one was perfect. It weighed only one kilogram, and the seller said the battery could last for ten hours. It cost eight million five hundred thousand som.

Dilnoza was worried about one thing. "Will it be fast enough for my video lessons?" she asked. The seller smiled and showed her how quickly it opened ten programs at the same time. Rustam also checked that it had a good keyboard, because Dilnoza types a lot.

She bought the third laptop and a small blue bag for it. On the way home she was so happy that she could not stop talking. In the evening she copied her old files to the new computer, and it took only twenty minutes.

Now Dilnoza uses the laptop every day. She is going to buy a wireless mouse next month, because she does not like the touchpad. She finishes her homework faster and has more free time for reading and walking in the park with her friends.

items.prompt: Where does Jack come from?
items.passage:
Jack is a sixteen-year-old student from Manchester. Two months ago he looked at his phone settings and got a surprise. The phone showed that he spent six hours a day on social media. "Six hours!" he said to his sister Amy. "That is almost a full school day."

Jack decided to change his habits. First, he checked which apps he used most. Video apps took three hours, and chatting with friends took two hours. The last hour was for photos and news. He understood that he was watching many short videos without thinking, and often he forgot why he had picked up the phone.

He made a simple plan. He set a time limit of two hours for all social media apps. When the limit ended, the phone showed a message and the apps closed. At first it was difficult, and he broke the rule on the second day. But he did not give up. He also stopped taking the phone to his bedroom. Instead, he bought a small alarm clock for seven pounds and left the phone in the kitchen at night.

After three weeks Jack noticed some good changes. He was sleeping better, and he felt less tired in the morning. His grades improved too, because he had more time for homework. He started playing football again with his friends on Tuesdays and Thursdays. "I did not know I had so much free time," he told Amy.

However, the change was not perfect. Some of his friends were using a group chat to plan the weekend, and Jack sometimes missed the news. Last Saturday he did not know about a birthday party until the afternoon. Now he checks the group chat once in the evening, and this works well.

Amy was impressed. She is thirteen, and she has decided to try the same plan. "If my brother can do it, I can do it too," she says. Their parents are very proud of both of them.

items.prompt: How long is the bus journey from Samarkand to the village?
items.passage:
Bobur lives in Samarkand, and his grandmother lives in a small village near Bukhara. They do not see each other often, because the journey takes about four hours by bus. Last Sunday, Bobur organised a video call for the whole family. It was his grandmother's seventieth birthday, and everyone wanted to say hello.

The day before the call, Bobur went to the village to help her. He brought an old tablet that his father did not use any more. He put it on the kitchen table and showed his grandmother how to answer a call. She was nervous. "What if I press the wrong button?" she asked. Bobur drew a big green circle on a piece of paper and put it next to the screen. "Just touch the green button," he said, and she laughed.

On Sunday at six o'clock in the evening, the call began. The first problem was the internet. The picture was frozen, and nobody could hear anything. Bobur's uncle Karim, who was in Moscow, said that the connection was weak. Bobur asked his grandmother to move the tablet closer to the window, and the picture became clear at once.

Eleven relatives joined the call from five different cities. Bobur's little cousin Zebo sang a birthday song, and his aunt showed the cake she had made. Grandmother was so happy that she cried a little. She said it was the best present she had ever received, even better than the warm scarf from last year.

The call lasted two hours. At the end, everyone promised to talk every month. Bobur told his grandmother, "I will call you next Sunday, and we can have tea together on the screen." She answered, "I would like that very much. Now I am not afraid of the green button."

After the call, Bobur felt proud. He had learned that technology can bring people together, even when they live far away.

items.prompt: Where does Emma work?
items.passage:
Emma works in a small travel office in Leeds. On Monday morning she arrived at work, turned on her computer and typed her password. Nothing happened. She typed it again, more slowly. The screen said, "Wrong password. You have two more tries." Emma felt a cold feeling in her stomach.

She had changed the password only two weeks before, because the office manager, Mr Hughes, had asked everyone to make safer passwords. Emma had chosen a long one with numbers and a capital letter, but she had not written it down. She thought she would remember it easily. Now she could not remember the last number.

She did not want to lock the computer, so she stopped. She called Tom from the technology team. Tom was friendly but busy. "I am in a meeting until eleven," he said. "Can you wait?" Emma could not wait, because a customer was coming at ten to book a holiday to Greece.

Then she remembered that the system had a reset button. She clicked on it, and the computer sent a message to her phone with a code of six numbers. She typed the code, and a new page opened. This time she chose a password that was easy to remember but still strong: the name of her dog, Biscuit, and her birthday. Then she wrote a small hint in her notebook, not the whole password.

She finished just in time. The customer, a man called Mr Davies, arrived at five to ten and booked a trip for his family. He paid by card, and Emma printed all the tickets.

Later Tom came to her desk and explained some rules. "Never use the same password for two accounts," he said. "And use a password manager if you can. It remembers everything for you." Emma thanked him. She has already started to use one, and she says she will never worry about a lost password again.

items.prompt: What is Aziz's job?
items.passage:
Aziz is a twenty-eight-year-old accountant who sits at a desk for most of the day. Last winter his doctor told him, "You must move more. Try to walk at least eight thousand steps every day." Aziz promised to try, but he did not know how to count his steps. His sister Malika had a good idea. For his birthday she gave him a smartwatch.

At first Aziz thought it was just a toy. The watch was black, light and comfortable, and it cost about two hundred dollars. But after the first week, he changed his mind. The watch counted his steps, measured his heartbeat and even showed how well he slept. On the first day he walked only three thousand steps, and he was a little ashamed.

So he began to change his routine. He started to get off the bus two stops earlier and walked the rest of the way to the office. He took the stairs instead of the lift. At lunch time he went for a short walk with his colleague Bekzod. The watch gave him small prizes on the screen when he reached his goal, and Aziz was surprised how much he enjoyed them.

After two months, he was walking ten thousand steps a day. His heartbeat was lower when he was resting, and he was sleeping about an hour longer. His doctor was pleased. "Keep going," she said, "but do not forget to rest."

There were also some problems. The battery lasted only two days, so Aziz had to charge the watch every other night. Once he forgot, and the watch stopped in the middle of a long walk. Another time it gave him a message at midnight, which woke him up.

Despite these problems, Aziz says the watch was the best present he has ever received. Next month he is going to run a five-kilometre race with Malika, and he feels ready.

At first Aziz thought it was just a toy. The watch was black, light and comfortable, and it cost about two hundred dollars. But after the first week, he changed his mind. The watch counted his steps, measured his heartbeat and even showed how well he slept. On the first day he walked only three thousand steps, and he was a little ashamed.

So he began to change his routine. He started to get off the bus two stops earlier and walked the rest of the way to the office. He took the stairs instead of the lift. At lunch time he went for a short walk with his colleague Bekzod. The watch gave him small prizes on the screen when he reached his goal, and Aziz was surprised how much he enjoyed them.

After two months, he was walking ten thousand steps a day. His heartbeat was lower when he was resting, and he was sleeping about an hour longer. His doctor was pleased. "Keep going," she said, "but do not forget to rest."

There were also some problems. The battery lasted only two days, so Aziz had to charge the watch every other night. Once he forgot, and the watch stopped in the middle of a long walk. Another time it gave him a message at midnight, which woke him up.

Despite these problems, Aziz says the watch was the best present he has ever received. Next month he is going to run a five-kilometre race with Malika, and he feels ready.

items.prompt: What kind of game does Sardor like most?
items.passage:
Sardor is fifteen, and he loves online games. His favourite game is a football game that he plays with three friends from his class: Javlon, Ali and Kamran. They usually play on Friday and Saturday evenings. In the game, they are a team, and they talk to each other through headphones.

The boys started playing together a year ago. At first they were not very good. They lost most of their matches, and sometimes they argued about who made the mistakes. Then Javlon suggested a new rule: "Nobody is allowed to shout. We must say what we see, and we must help each other." The rule worked. Within a month, they won ten games in a row and moved up to a higher level.

Sardor's mother, Gulnora, was worried at first. She thought the games were a waste of time, and she was afraid that her son would not do his homework. One evening she sat next to him and watched a match. She was surprised. "You need to think fast," she said, "and you work as a team. It is almost like a real sport." After that, she made a deal with Sardor. He could play for two hours on weekend evenings, but only after he finished his homework and tidied his room.

There are some dangers, of course. Sardor knows that he should never give his real name or address to strangers in the game. Last month a player he did not know asked him for his phone number. Sardor refused and told his teacher about it the next day. The teacher thanked him and said he had done the right thing.

Now the team is training for a school tournament in April. The winners will get a small cup and a voucher for a pizza restaurant. Sardor says that winning is not the most important thing. "I just enjoy playing with my friends," he says, "and I have learned to stay calm when things go wrong."

items.prompt: How old was Nigora's phone?
items.passage:
Nigora's phone was only two years old, but its battery was terrible. In the morning it showed a hundred per cent, and by lunch time it showed twenty. Last Thursday it died at three o'clock, just when she was waiting for an important message from her university teacher.

Nigora was angry. She thought about buying a new phone, but it was too expensive. Then her friend Sevara said, "Wait. Maybe the problem is not the battery. Maybe you are using the phone in a wrong way." She looked at Nigora's screen and laughed. "Your screen is so bright! And you have more than thirty apps working in the background."

They sat down together and made some changes. First, Sevara reduced the brightness of the screen by half. Then she closed the apps that Nigora never used, like three old games and a weather app. She also turned off the location service for most programs. "They follow you all day and use a lot of power," Sevara explained. Finally, she showed Nigora a small button that saves energy when the battery is low.

The next day, Nigora left home at eight o'clock with eighty-five per cent. When she came home at seven in the evening, there was still thirty per cent left. She could not believe it. "It is much better than before!" she told Sevara on the phone.

Sevara also gave her some advice. "Do not charge the phone to a hundred per cent every night. It is better to stop at about eighty. And never leave it in a hot place, for example on a sunny window." Nigora wrote the tips in her notebook.

Now she carries a small cable in her bag, but she does not need it very often. She has decided to keep her old phone for another year. "I saved a lot of money," she says, "and all I did was change a few settings."

items.prompt: Where do the Browns live?
items.passage:
Mr and Mrs Brown live in a small house in Bristol with their two children and a big dog called Max. The house is always full of dust and hair, and cleaning it took Mrs Brown nearly an hour every day. Last spring, Mr Brown decided to surprise his wife. He bought a robot vacuum cleaner for three hundred pounds.

The robot was round, grey and about as big as a large plate. Mr Brown put it in the middle of the living room, pressed a button and said, "Watch this." The robot made a quiet noise and began to move. It went under the sofa, around the table and along the walls. Max was frightened, and he ran into the kitchen. The children, Ella and Sam, laughed and followed the robot everywhere.

The first week was not easy. The robot got stuck under the bed twice, and once it ate a sock. Another time, it went up the stairs and could not come down, so Mr Brown had to carry it. Mrs Brown was not impressed. "It is more work than the old vacuum cleaner," she said.

But Mr Brown did not give up. He read the instructions and found out that the robot had a phone app. With the app, they could draw a map of the house and tell the robot not to go to the stairs. They also set a time: every morning at nine o'clock, when everyone was out. After that, things became much easier.

Now the floors are cleaner than they were before, and Mrs Brown has an extra hour in her day. She uses it to read or drink tea in the garden. Max has become friends with the robot, and he sometimes sleeps next to it when it is charging.

Mrs Brown has changed her opinion. "At first I thought it was a silly present," she says, "but now I would not clean without it."

items.prompt: What is the name of the TV series?
items.passage:
Kamola is a nineteen-year-old student of languages in Tashkent. Three weeks ago her friend Dildora told her about a British TV series called "The Harbour". It has forty episodes, and each one lasts about forty-five minutes. "It is a great way to practise English," Dildora said, "and the story is really exciting."

Kamola decided to try it. The series is about a family who run a small hotel in a fishing town in Cornwall. In the first episode, the father, Mr Penrose, finds a mysterious letter in an old box. The letter tells about a hidden treasure that was lost in a storm in nineteen twenty. From that moment, every episode brings a new secret.

At first Kamola found the series very difficult. The actors spoke fast and used a strange accent. She turned on the English subtitles, and that helped a lot. After five episodes she could follow the story without stopping the video every minute. items.prompt: What is Oliver's job?
items.passage:
Oliver is a thirty-five-year-old bus driver from Glasgow. He spends about six hours a day in his bus, and for years he listened to the radio. Last year, however, his daughter Chloe showed him how to find podcasts on his phone. "You can listen to anything you like, Dad," she said, "and whenever you want."

Oliver began with a podcast about history. Each episode was thirty minutes long, and the host, a woman called Dr Fraser, told a story about a famous person or event. Oliver loved it. He learned about Roman roads, Viking ships and the first train in Scotland. Sometimes he arrived at the bus station and did not want to stop the story, so he sat in the bus for five more minutes.

Soon he wanted to hear more, so he found a podcast about cooking, and another one about football. He listened to a new episode every morning and every afternoon. Passengers noticed that he was happier. "You always smile now," an old lady told him one day. "Before you looked tired."

Then Oliver had an idea. He knew a lot of funny stories about the people he met on his bus, and he decided to make his own podcast. Chloe helped him to buy a small microphone for twenty pounds and showed him how to record on his laptop. The first episode, called "Route Forty-Two", was only ten minutes long. Oliver was so nervous that he recorded it six times.

To his surprise, three hundred people listened to the first episode in one week. Some of them wrote friendly comments, and one man even asked him for a second episode about the night buses. Oliver is now preparing one.

"I never thought I would be a podcaster," he says. "I just wanted something to listen to, and now I am making something for other people." He says the best part of his job is that every day brings a new story.

Oliver began with a podcast about history. Each episode was thirty minutes long, and the host, a woman called Dr Fraser, told a story about a famous person or event. Oliver loved it. He learned about Roman roads, Viking ships and the first train in Scotland. Sometimes he arrived at the bus station and did not want to stop the story, so he sat in the bus for five more minutes.

Soon he wanted to hear more, so he found a podcast about cooking, and another one about football. He listened to a new episode every morning and every afternoon. Passengers noticed that he was happier. "You always smile now," an old lady told him one day. "Before you looked tired."

Then Oliver had an idea. He knew a lot of funny stories about the people he met on his bus, and he decided to make his own podcast. Chloe helped him to buy a small microphone for twenty pounds and showed him how to record on his laptop. The first episode, called "Route Forty-Two", was only ten minutes long. Oliver was so nervous that he recorded it six times.

To his surprise, three hundred people listened to the first episode in one week. Some of them wrote friendly comments, and one man even asked him for a second episode about the night buses. Oliver is now preparing one.

"I never thought I would be a podcaster," he says. "I just wanted something to listen to, and now I am making something for other people." He says the best part of his job is that every day brings a new story.

items.prompt: What kind of company does Lola work for?
items.passage:
Lola works as an assistant in an advertising company in Tashkent. She likes her job, and she is usually very careful. But last Wednesday she made a mistake that she will never forget.

In the morning, her manager, Mr Rashidov, asked her to send a report to a new client, a large furniture company. The report included prices, plans and some private information about other customers. Lola prepared the report, wrote a polite message and clicked "send". Only then did she see the problem. She had chosen the wrong address. Instead of sending it to the furniture company, she had sent it to the whole list of customers, more than two hundred people.

Lola felt her heart beating fast. She did not know what to do. She stood up, walked to the window and took a deep breath. Then she went straight to Mr Rashidov's office and told him the truth. "I have made a terrible mistake," she said. "I am so sorry."

Mr Rashidov was not happy, but he stayed calm. "Thank you for telling me at once," he said. "It is better than hiding it." He called the technology team, and they tried to stop the message. It was too late for some people, but they managed to delete it from about half of the inboxes. Then Mr Rashidov wrote a short apology to every customer and asked them to delete the email.

By the end of the day, most of the customers had answered kindly. A few of them even said that everybody makes mistakes. The furniture company received the correct report on Thursday morning and signed the contract on Friday.

Since then, Lola has used a new system. She reads the address twice, and she waits ten seconds before she presses the button. She has also put a note on her screen that says, "Check. Then send." She says the lesson was expensive, but it taught her to be more careful.

items.prompt: Who gave Timur the 3D printer?
items.passage:
Timur is fourteen, and he is crazy about technology. For his birthday in January, his uncle Jamshid gave him a small 3D printer. Timur could not believe it. He had seen such machines only on the internet, and he had always wanted to try one.

The first week was difficult. The printer needed to be put together, and the instructions were long. Timur and his uncle worked for two evenings and finally finished. Then they chose a simple model, a small blue cup, and pressed the start button. The printer began to build the cup layer by layer. It took three hours, and Timur did not leave the room for a minute. When it was ready, the cup was a little rough, but he was extremely proud.

He soon learned that making things is not as easy as it looks. His second project, a phone stand, broke when he put his phone on it. His third project, a toy car for his little brother Nodir, had no wheels, because he forgot to make them. But every mistake taught him something new. He learned to change the temperature of the machine, to use less plastic and to check the size of each part.

After two months, Timur could design his own objects on the computer. He made a pencil holder for his school desk, a small box for his mother's rings and a key ring with his name on it. His classmates were impressed, and a few of them asked him to make something for them. His friend Eldor paid him two dollars for a key ring.

Timur's teacher heard about the printer and invited him to give a short talk in the science club. He showed the cup, the toy car and the pencil holder. Many students asked questions.

Now Timur dreams about becoming an engineer. "With a 3D printer you can make almost anything," he says. "You only need an idea and some patience."

items.prompt: What is Farhod's job?
items.passage:
Farhod is a photographer who lives in the mountains near Chimgan. Last summer he bought a small drone, because he wanted to take pictures of the landscape from above. The drone was white, light and about as big as a loaf of bread. It cost six hundred dollars, and Farhod had saved for almost a year.

Before his first flight, he read the rules carefully. In Uzbekistan, you must not fly a drone near airports, and you must keep it in sight at all times. You also need to be careful in places with many people. Farhod learned that he should fly under a hundred and twenty metres. He also checked the weather, because strong wind can be dangerous for small drones.

On Saturday morning he went to a quiet field near his house. The weather was perfect, with no wind and a clear blue sky. Farhod put the drone on the ground, held the controller and pressed the button. The drone rose slowly into the air with a soft buzzing noise. He was very nervous, and his hands were shaking. But after ten minutes he felt more confident.

The pictures were wonderful. From above, the mountains looked even bigger than usual, and the river looked like a silver line in the green valley. Farhod took more than two hundred photos in one hour. He also made a short film, which he showed to his friends in the evening. They all asked him to teach them.

There was one small accident. On the second flight, the drone flew into a tree and fell to the ground. Fortunately, only one propeller was broken, and Farhod bought a new one for five dollars. He now practises every weekend, and his flying is much better than it was in the beginning.

Next month a travel magazine is going to publish three of his photos. "A drone has changed my work," Farhod says. "I can show people places that they have never seen before."

items.prompt: What was Madina's first video about?
items.passage:
Madina is seventeen years old and loves cooking. Two years ago she decided to start a channel on the internet where she shows easy recipes for students. Her first video was about how to make plov in a small pot. She filmed it in the kitchen with her mother's old phone, and she put it online on a Sunday evening.

Nobody watched it. After a week, the video had only eleven views, and nine of them were from her family. Madina was disappointed, but her older brother Anvar gave her some advice. "Your idea is good," he said, "but the sound is bad and the light is dark. Buy a cheap microphone and film near the window." Madina followed his advice, and her second video looked much better.

Slowly the channel started to grow. After three months, it had two hundred followers. Madina learned to write a short title that people want to click on, and she learned to cut the long, boring parts of the film. She published one new video every Saturday, and she always answered the comments.

The big change came last spring. A video called "Breakfast in five minutes" was shared by a famous food blogger, and in one week it had sixty thousand views. Madina could not sleep that night, because her phone showed new messages every minute. She now has more than twenty thousand followers.

Success has not made her life easier. She still goes to school, and she spends most of her free time planning, shopping, filming and cutting. Sometimes she gets mean comments, which make her sad. Her mother tells her, "Read the nice ones and forget the others."

Madina is not planning to stop. Next year she wants to study food technology and write a small cookbook. "A channel is not only about being famous," she says. "It is about sharing something you love with people you do not know."

items.prompt: How old is Mr Walker?
items.passage:
Mr Walker is sixty-eight years old, and he has always used cash. For forty years he went to the same bank in the town centre every Friday morning, stood in a queue and paid his bills. Last year, however, the bank closed that branch, and the nearest one was now eight kilometres away.

His grandson Harry, who is twenty-one, said, "Grandad, you should try online banking. It is easy and safe, and you can do everything from home." Mr Walker was not sure. He read in the newspaper about people who lost money on the internet, and he did not trust his computer. "I will think about it," he said.

A month later, he gave in. On a rainy Saturday, Harry came to his house and they sat together in front of the laptop. First, they opened an account on the bank's website. Harry explained that Mr Walker must never tell anyone his password, not even a person who calls from the bank. "The bank will never ask you for it," he said. Then they connected the account to Mr Walker's phone, so that he receives a code every time he logs in.

They practised paying the electricity bill. Mr Walker typed slowly with two fingers, and it took him twenty minutes. But when he pressed the last button, a green message appeared on the screen: "Payment successful". He was delighted. "No queue, no bus, no rain," he said.

Now Mr Walker does his banking every Friday at ten o'clock, with a cup of tea. He pays his bills in five minutes and checks his savings. He has also learned to recognise false messages. Last week, he received an email that said, "Your account is closed. Click here." He deleted it at once and told Harry about it.

Mr Walker tells his friends at the club that online banking is better than he expected. "Sometimes you just have to try something new," he says, "even when you are sixty-eight."

items.prompt: How many exams did Dilnoza have?
items.passage:
Dilnoza is sixteen and she goes to School Number Twelve in Samarkand. Last week was exam week, and it was the most tiring week of her year. She had four exams: maths on Monday, history on Tuesday, English on Thursday and chemistry on Friday. For two weeks before that, she had studied every evening after dinner, usually from seven o'clock until ten.

On Sunday night, Dilnoza felt very nervous. Her younger brother Jamshid was playing a loud computer game in the next room, so she could not concentrate. She asked him politely to stop, but he did not listen. In the end, she took her notebooks to the kitchen, where her mother was making tea. They sat together for an hour, and her mother tested her on the history dates. This helped her a lot, and she went to bed at half past ten.

The maths exam was harder than she had expected. There were twelve questions, and she could not solve the last two. When she left the classroom, her friend Madina was smiling, but Dilnoza was worried. However, her teacher, Mrs Rustamova, told her the next day that she had got seventy-eight out of one hundred. That was better than her last result, which was sixty-nine.

The history exam was her favourite. She wrote a long answer about the Silk Road and remembered almost every date. On Thursday, the English test had a listening part, and the recording was so fast that many students missed some answers. Dilnoza did not panic. She wrote what she understood and then checked her spelling carefully. Chemistry was the last exam, and her hands were shaking when she began.

On Friday afternoon, all the students were free. Dilnoza and Madina walked to the park and bought ice cream. They were tired but happy. Dilnoza promised herself that next time she would start studying earlier and sleep more. The results will be on the school website in ten days, and she hopes to get good marks in all four subjects.

items.prompt: How long was the flight from Tashkent?
items.passage:
In April, Bobur's class took a school trip to Istanbul in Turkey. There were twenty-four students and three teachers, and it was the first time Bobur had travelled by plane. The flight from Tashkent took four hours. Bobur sat next to the window, and he watched the clouds for most of the journey. His friend Sardor was afraid of flying, so he held a book and did not look outside.

The group stayed in a small hotel near the Blue Mosque for five nights. Every morning, they had breakfast at eight o'clock and then met their guide, a friendly woman called Elif. She spoke very good English and told them many stories about the old city. On the second day, they visited the Grand Bazaar, which has more than four thousand shops. Bobur wanted to buy a present for his mother, and he finally chose a blue scarf for fifteen lira.

The best day was Wednesday, when the class took a boat trip on the Bosphorus. The weather was sunny but windy, and some students felt cold. A teacher, Mr Aliyev, was taking photographs when his hat suddenly flew into the water. Everybody laughed, and a sailor even tried to catch it with a long stick, but he failed. Later, Mr Aliyev bought a new hat and joked that Istanbul was an expensive city for hats.

There were also some small problems. On the third evening, the students were so tired that two of them fell asleep during dinner. Another boy lost his phone, but the hotel manager found it the next morning under a chair. Bobur learned a few Turkish words, such as teshekkurler, which means thank you.

On the last day, the class had a short lesson in a Turkish school and met some local students. They exchanged email addresses and promised to write. Bobur says that the trip was the best week of his life, and he wants to travel to another country next year.

items.prompt: How long did the students have for the project?
items.passage:
Last month, Aziza and her partner Oliver had to make a science project for their class. Their teacher, Ms Parker, gave the students three weeks and one simple question to answer. Aziza and Oliver chose the question: do plants grow better in light or in the dark? They thought the answer was easy, but the experiment taught them many surprising things.

First, they bought twelve small bean seeds and six plastic pots. They put soil in each pot and planted two seeds. Three pots stayed on the window of Aziza's kitchen, where there was a lot of sunlight. The other three went into a cupboard in the living room, where it was completely dark. Every morning before school, they gave each pot exactly fifty millilitres of water, and every evening they measured the plants with a ruler.

After one week, the plants in the cupboard were already taller than the plants on the window. Oliver was confused. He said, "I thought light would help them to grow faster!" Aziza looked at the plants closely and noticed that the dark plants were thin, weak and almost white. The plants from the window were shorter, but they were thick and bright green. She told Oliver that the dark plants were growing very fast because they were looking for light.

At the end of the third week, the pair wrote a report and made a poster with photographs and a graph. The tallest plant in the dark was twenty-eight centimetres, and the tallest plant on the window was nineteen centimetres. items.prompt: What subject did Mr Hashimov teach?
items.passage:
When Kamila was twelve, she had the strictest teacher in her school. His name was Mr Hashimov, and he taught mathematics. Everybody in the school knew his rules. Students had to arrive five minutes before the lesson, they could not use their phones, and they had to do their homework in a blue pen. If somebody was late, they had to stand at the back of the room for the whole lesson.

At first, Kamila hated his classes. Mr Hashimov never smiled, and he spoke in a very low, serious voice. Once, she forgot her notebook, and he made her write the whole lesson on a piece of paper. She went home crying and told her father that she wanted to change schools. Her father listened carefully and said, "Wait one more month. Perhaps he is not as bad as you think."

A few weeks later, something changed. Kamila failed a test, and she was afraid to show it to her parents. After the lesson, Mr Hashimov asked her to stay. She expected a long speech, but he was surprisingly kind. He sat down beside her and explained every mistake slowly. Then he gave her extra exercises and offered to help her on Tuesdays and Thursdays after school. He said, "I am strict because I believe in you."

Kamila went to his extra classes for three months. Slowly, maths became easier, and her marks went up from fifty-eight to eighty-five. She also noticed that Mr Hashimov was funny in a quiet way. He sometimes wrote little jokes at the bottom of the board, and only the students who read carefully could find them.

Now Kamila is twenty-two and works as a teacher herself. She says that strict teachers are often the ones we remember best. Last year she visited the old school and thanked Mr Hashimov. He smiled for the first time, and she almost did not recognise him.

Students had to arrive five minutes before the lesson, they could not use their phones, and they had to do their homework in a blue pen. If somebody was late, they had to stand at the back of the room for the whole lesson.

At first, Kamila hated his classes. Mr Hashimov never smiled, and he spoke in a very low, serious voice. Once, she forgot her notebook, and he made her write the whole lesson on a piece of paper. She went home crying and told her father that she wanted to change schools. Her father listened carefully and said, "Wait one more month. Perhaps he is not as bad as you think."

A few weeks later, something changed. Kamila failed a test, and she was afraid to show it to her parents. After the lesson, Mr Hashimov asked her to stay. She expected a long speech, but he was surprisingly kind. He sat down beside her and explained every mistake slowly. Then he gave her extra exercises and offered to help her on Tuesdays and Thursdays after school. He said, "I am strict because I believe in you."

Kamila went to his extra classes for three months. Slowly, maths became easier, and her marks went up from fifty-eight to eighty-five. She also noticed that Mr Hashimov was funny in a quiet way. He sometimes wrote little jokes at the bottom of the board, and only the students who read carefully could find them.

Now Kamila is twenty-two and works as a teacher herself. She says that strict teachers are often the ones we remember best. Last year she visited the old school and thanked Mr Hashimov. He smiled for the first time, and she almost did not recognise him.

items.prompt: What was the name of the play?
items.passage:
Every December, the students of Lyceum Seven perform a play for their parents. This year, the drama teacher, Mrs Nazarova, chose a story called The Lost Crown. It was a funny adventure about a prince, a clever girl and three silly guards. Thirty students wanted a part, but there were only fourteen roles. Mrs Nazarova organised auditions on a Monday afternoon.

Malika was fifteen and very shy, but she really wanted to play the clever girl. She practised her lines in front of the mirror for a whole week. On the day of the audition, her voice was so quiet that the teacher asked her to repeat it twice. Malika thought she had failed. However, the next morning, she saw her name next to the main role on the notice board. She was so surprised that she dropped her bag.

The rehearsals were hard. They met three times a week after lessons, and each rehearsal lasted two hours. The boy who played the prince, Rustam, kept forgetting his words, and the three guards could not stop laughing. Mrs Nazarova was patient, but one day she shouted, "If you laugh again, I will cancel the play!" Everybody became quiet immediately.

Two days before the show, a big problem appeared. The costume for the prince was too small, and nobody could find a crown. Malika's grandmother, who is a good tailor, made a new costume in one evening. The crown was made from yellow paper and gold paint by two students from the art club.

On the evening of the play, the hall was full. There were more than two hundred people. Malika was terribly nervous, but when she stepped onto the stage, she forgot her fear. The audience laughed at the guards and clapped loudly at the end. Afterwards, her father gave her a bunch of flowers, and she said it was the happiest night of her life.

items.prompt: How did the children travel to the university?
items.passage:
On a sunny Saturday in March, Javlon and his sister Sevara went to the open day at the National University in Tashkent. Javlon is seventeen and wants to study computer science, while Sevara, who is fifteen, only came because her brother asked her. They left home at eight o'clock and took the metro, then walked for ten minutes to the main gate.

At the entrance, a student volunteer called Anvar gave them a map and a programme. The day started with a welcome talk at nine thirty in the big hall, where the rector spoke about the history of the university. It was founded in nineteen eighteen and now has about thirty thousand students. Javlon found the talk a little boring, but Sevara liked the part about the exchange programmes with universities in Korea and Germany.

After the talk, the visitors could choose a tour. Javlon joined the computer science group. The guide showed them a laboratory with new computers and a small robot that could carry cups of tea. Javlon asked how difficult the first year was. The guide answered honestly: the course was hard, but students who worked regularly usually passed. Meanwhile, Sevara visited the library, which is open until midnight during exams, and she was impressed by the quiet study rooms.

At one o'clock, they had lunch in the student cafe. The food was cheap, and a plate of plov cost only twenty thousand sum. They sat with two first-year students, who gave them useful advice: choose a subject you love, and join a club in the first month.

In the afternoon, Javlon collected leaflets about scholarships and entrance exams. On the way home, he said that he was now sure about his choice. Sevara laughed and said that the university was nicer than she had expected. She might apply there too, in two years.

items.prompt: Why did Nigora start the study group?
items.passage:
Three months ago, Nigora started a study group at her college. She was having problems with physics, and she knew that two of her classmates, Timur and Laylo, felt the same. One Monday, she wrote a message in the class chat: "Let's study together on Wednesdays at four o'clock in the library. Who wants to join?" By the evening, seven people had answered yes.

The first meeting was a little chaotic. Everybody brought different books, and nobody knew what to study. Timur wanted to talk about electricity, but Laylo preferred to revise the chapter on light. After twenty minutes of arguing, Nigora took a piece of paper and made a plan. Each week, one person would prepare a short explanation of one topic and teach it to the others. The rest of the group would ask questions and then solve five exercises together.

The idea worked better than anyone expected. When Timur explained electricity, he used a funny example with water in a pipe, and everybody understood it at once. Laylo drew colourful pictures on the board. Nigora herself discovered that teaching was the best way to learn. "When I have to explain something, I find out what I don't really know," she said.

There were some rules. Phones had to stay in bags, and the group could eat only fruit or nuts. Anyone who came late had to bring a snack for the next meeting. Timur was late twice, so he brought apples and then walnuts.

At the end of the term, the group had a physics test. Nigora got eighty-nine points, Timur got eighty-four and Laylo got ninety-two, which was her best result ever. They were all delighted. Now the group has twelve members and meets twice a week, and they have started a second group for chemistry.

items.prompt: How did Gulnora get a place at the summer school?
items.passage:
Last July, Gulnora, a seventeen-year-old student from Bukhara, spent three weeks at a summer school in Edinburgh, Scotland. She had won a place in an English competition, and the prize included the course, the flight and a room in a student house. It was her first time abroad, and she was both excited and frightened when the plane took off.

The school had students from fourteen countries, including Italy, Brazil, Japan and Poland. In the first lesson, the teacher, a young Scottish man called Callum, asked everybody to say three things about themselves. Gulnora was nervous, but she told the class that she liked chess, hated spiders and could cook a very good plov. The students laughed, and she immediately felt more relaxed.

Lessons started at nine and finished at one o'clock. In the afternoons, there were activities: football, a visit to the castle, a film evening and a trip to the sea. Gulnora's favourite activity was a walk up a big hill called Arthur's Seat. It took them an hour, and the view of the city from the top was beautiful. Unfortunately, it began to rain, and everybody got wet. They laughed all the way down the hill.

She also had some difficulties. At first, she could not understand the Scottish accent, and she asked Callum to repeat everything. The food was strange for her, too. She did not like porridge in the morning, but she loved the fresh fish. Her roommate, a girl from Italy called Chiara, taught her some Italian words and shared biscuits with her.

On the last Friday, each student gave a five-minute talk about their country. Gulnora spoke about the old streets of Bukhara and brought a little bag of dried apricots for everyone. She says that her English improved more in three weeks than in a whole year at school, and she hopes to return to Scotland one day.

items.prompt: Who practised with Ibrohim every evening?
items.passage:
The school spelling contest takes place every spring in the town of Namangan. This year, ten-year-old Ibrohim represented his class, and he was very nervous. He had practised with his older sister Zarina every evening for a month. She read difficult words from a dictionary, and he wrote them down. At first, he made many mistakes, but by the end of March he could spell almost every word correctly.

The contest was held in the school hall on a Saturday morning. There were forty children from eight different schools, and the judge was a tall lady with big glasses called Mrs Ergasheva. The rules were simple. Each child stood up, listened to a word and spelled it aloud. If the spelling was wrong, he or she had to sit down. The last child on the stage was the winner.

The first round was easy, with words like garden, window and friend. Ten children went out, though, because they forgot the double letters in words such as summer and yellow. In the second round, the words were harder: neighbour, island and enough. Ibrohim hesitated on neighbour, but he remembered the silent letters and spelled it correctly. His hands were cold, and he felt his heart beating fast.

After five rounds, only three children were left: Ibrohim, a girl called Dilfuza and a boy from another school named Akmal. Dilfuza made a mistake on the word necessary, and she left the stage with tears in her eyes. Then Ibrohim and Akmal spelled eleven more words each. Finally, Akmal could not spell the word restaurant, and Ibrohim got his last word, calendar, right.

The prize was a big dictionary and a certificate. Ibrohim was so happy that he ran to hug Zarina. She said she was not surprised, because he had worked harder than anybody. Next year, he plans to try again and, perhaps, to help his younger cousin to prepare.

items.prompt: How much did the driving school cost?
items.passage:
When Sherzod turned eighteen, his father said, "Now you can learn to drive." Sherzod had waited for this day for years. He found a driving school near his home, which charged four hundred thousand sum for twenty lessons. His instructor was a patient man called Mr Yusupov, who had taught driving for twenty-five years and said that he had never lost his temper.

The first lesson was in an empty car park on a Sunday morning. Sherzod learned how to start the engine, change gear and use the pedals. He was so careless that the car jumped forward and stopped suddenly three times. Mr Yusupov only smiled and said, "Everybody does that. Try again, slowly." By the end of the hour, Sherzod could drive in a straight line at ten kilometres per hour.

After the fifth lesson, they moved onto quiet streets. Sherzod found this much more stressful. There were cyclists, pedestrians and buses, and he had to look everywhere at once. One day, he forgot to check the mirror, and a motorbike passed very close to the car. His hands were shaking, but Mr Yusupov explained calmly that a good driver is not a fast driver, but a careful one.

The theory test was the part that Sherzod worried about most. He studied road signs every night for two weeks and did online practice tests on his phone. On the day of the test, he answered thirty-six questions correctly out of forty, which was enough to pass. His mother baked a cake to celebrate.

The practical test was one month later. It was raining, and Sherzod was afraid he would make a mistake in the parking part. However, he parked perfectly in his first try, and the examiner gave him the licence. His father let him drive home, and Sherzod drove very slowly and carefully all the way.

His instructor was a patient man called Mr Yusupov, who had taught driving for twenty-five years and said that he had never lost his temper.

The first lesson was in an empty car park on a Sunday morning. Sherzod learned how to start the engine, change gear and use the pedals. He was so careless that the car jumped forward and stopped suddenly three times. Mr Yusupov only smiled and said, "Everybody does that. Try again, slowly." By the end of the hour, Sherzod could drive in a straight line at ten kilometres per hour.

After the fifth lesson, they moved onto quiet streets. Sherzod found this much more stressful. There were cyclists, pedestrians and buses, and he had to look everywhere at once. One day, he forgot to check the mirror, and a motorbike passed very close to the car. His hands were shaking, but Mr Yusupov explained calmly that a good driver is not a fast driver, but a careful one.

The theory test was the part that Sherzod worried about most. He studied road signs every night for two weeks and did online practice tests on his phone. On the day of the test, he answered thirty-six questions correctly out of forty, which was enough to pass. His mother baked a cake to celebrate.

The practical test was one month later. It was raining, and Sherzod was afraid he would make a mistake in the parking part. However, he parked perfectly in his first try, and the examiner gave him the licence. His father let him drive home, and Sherzod drove very slowly and carefully all the way.

items.prompt: Why did the narrator interview Grandmother?
items.answer: The teacher asked for an interview
items.passage:
My grandmother, Halima, is seventy-eight years old, and she loves telling stories about her childhood. Last Sunday, I visited her with a notebook, because my teacher had asked us to interview an older person about school life in the past. We sat on her porch, drank green tea and talked for two hours.

Grandmother was born in a small village near Fergana. When she was seven, she started school. The school was one big room with a stove in the middle, and about thirty children of different ages studied together. In winter, every child had to bring a piece of wood for the stove. She remembers carrying heavy wood in the snow, and her fingers always felt like ice.

There were no computers, no phones and not many books. The children wrote with pens and a bottle of ink, and they often had blue fingers. Her favourite subject was singing, and her least favourite was arithmetic. The teacher, Mr Qodirov, was strict but fair. If somebody talked in class, he gave them extra homework, but he never shouted.

The road to school was three kilometres long, and she walked it every day with her cousin Zebo. They did not have shoes in summer, so they walked barefoot and sometimes stopped to swim in a stream. In the evenings, she helped her mother to bake bread and feed the chickens. She said that children did not have much free time, but they were never bored.

When I asked what she thought about school today, she smiled. She said that I was lucky to have warm classrooms, many books and the internet. However, she also said that children today spend too much time on their phones and too little time outside. Before I left, she gave me a small tin box with her old school photograph inside. I will take it to class and show it to everybody.

items.prompt: What does Mirzo's father do?
items.passage:
Mirzo comes from a small town in the Khorezm region, and his family is not rich. His father is a bus driver, and his mother works in a bakery. Mirzo has always been good at mathematics, but until last year he did not think that he could study abroad. Then his teacher, Mr Saidov, told him about a scholarship for talented students at a university in Malaysia.

The application was not easy. Mirzo had to fill in a long form, write an essay about his dreams and send two letters from teachers. He also had to take an English test. His English was not very good then, so he started to study every day. He listened to English podcasts on the bus, learned ten new words each morning and practised speaking with his cousin on the phone.

The essay was the hardest part. He wrote five different versions, and he threw four of them away. In the final one, he described how he repaired the old computer of his school and taught younger children to use it. Mr Saidov read it and said, "This is honest, and it sounds like you." Mirzo posted the whole package in September, and then he had to wait.

The answer came in December. At first, Mirzo thought that it was an advertisement and almost deleted the email. When he read it carefully, he saw the words, "We are pleased to offer you a full scholarship." He ran to the kitchen and showed it to his mother, who started to cry with joy. His father could not speak for a minute, and then he hugged his son so hard that Mirzo could not breathe.

Mirzo will start his studies next August. He will study engineering, and the scholarship will pay for his tuition, his room and one flight home every year. He says that he will work hard, because many people believed in him.

items.prompt: Where does Lukas come from?
items.passage:
In September, a new student joined our class. His name was Lukas, and he came from Germany for one school year as an exchange student. He is seventeen, tall and a little shy, and at first he spoke only a few words of Uzbek. He lives with the family of our classmate Otabek, and he says that the best part of his day is dinner with them.

On his first day, our teacher asked Lukas to introduce himself. He said, "Salom, my name is Lukas. I like football, bicycles and cheese." Everybody laughed, because nobody expected him to mention cheese. After the lesson, Otabek and I invited him to play football with us. He turned out to be an excellent goalkeeper, and since then he has played with our team every Friday.

Lukas has found many things in Uzbekistan very different from home. In Germany, students finish school at one o'clock and have lunch at home, but here we stay until two thirty. He was also surprised that we stand up when the teacher enters the room. He told us that in his school students stay in their seats and call the teachers by their first names. We thought this sounded strange, and he thought our habits were strange too, so we laughed together.

The food was a big adventure. Otabek's mother cooked plov, manti and samsa, and Lukas ate so much that he could hardly walk. His favourite dish is lagman. He has already learned to make it, and last month he cooked it for his host family. Unfortunately, he put too much salt in it, but they ate it politely.

Lukas has been here for three months now, and his Uzbek is improving fast. He can order food, ask for directions and even tell a joke. In June, he will go back to Germany, and many of us will feel sad. We have promised to visit him in Berlin, and he has promised to teach us German cheese songs.

items.prompt: Who suggested that Feruza join the debate club?
items.passage:
Last autumn, Feruza joined the debate club at her school. She had never spoken in front of a large group, and she was afraid of it, but her English teacher, Ms Collins, said that debating was the best way to improve confidence. The club met every Thursday after lessons in Room Fourteen and had eleven members.

In a debate, two teams argue about a statement. One team agrees, and the other team disagrees. Each speaker has three minutes, and a judge decides who wins. The first topic Feruza had was "Homework should be banned." She was in the team that disagreed. At the start, she felt sick, and her hands were wet. She spoke for only one minute and forgot most of her notes. Her team lost the debate, and she wanted to leave the club.

Ms Collins, however, encouraged her. She told Feruza that all good speakers had been bad speakers once, and she gave her three tips: breathe slowly, look at one friendly face and use short sentences. Feruza practised every night in front of her cat, who was not very interested but never interrupted.

By December, she was much better. In the school tournament, her team had to argue that students should wear uniforms. Feruza gave the second speech and talked for exactly three minutes. She used a good example about two girls who spent an hour every morning choosing clothes. The judges smiled, and her team won by two points.

items.prompt: What time did the narrator wake up?
items.passage:
Graduation day at our school was on the twenty-fifth of May, and I will remember it for the rest of my life. I woke up at six o'clock, which was far too early, because I could not sleep with excitement. My mother had ironed my white shirt the night before, and my father was already polishing his shoes in the hall. Everybody in the house was nervous.

The ceremony began at ten o'clock in the school yard. There were colourful balloons on every tree, and the youngest students stood in two long lines with flowers in their hands. We, the graduates, walked slowly between them, wearing blue gowns and funny square hats. My friend Anora whispered that she was going to cry, and I told her not to, but I could feel my own eyes becoming wet.

The headmaster, Mr Tursunov, made a speech. He said that we had been a lively and sometimes noisy class, but also a kind one. He reminded us about the time when we collected money for a village library and bought two hundred books. Then each student received a certificate, and the teachers shook our hands. When my name was called, my knees were shaking so much that I nearly tripped on the stage.

After the certificates, our class teacher, Mrs Hamidova, gave a short, emotional talk. She had taught us for six years, and she said that she was proud of every one of us. Several students started crying, and she cried too. Then we gave her a big bunch of white roses and a photo album with pictures of all our trips and parties.

In the evening, there was a party in a restaurant with music and dancing. We danced until midnight, and then we walked through the quiet streets and watched the sunrise from the bridge. I felt sad to finish school, but also curious about the future. In September, I will begin to study medicine at university.

He reminded us about the time when we collected money for a village library and bought two hundred books. Then each student received a certificate, and the teachers shook our hands. items.prompt: Where did Madina's wedding take place?
items.passage:
Last Saturday my cousin Madina got married in Samarkand, and I helped my aunt Gulnora cook for the wedding feast. We started on Thursday morning at six o'clock because there were two hundred guests and a lot of work to do. My aunt had hired a famous cook, Ustoz Rustam, who was sixty years old and had cooked at weddings for forty years.

The first job was the plov. Rustam used eighty kilos of rice, fifty kilos of yellow carrots and forty kilos of lamb. He cooked it in a huge black kazan over a wood fire. While he was stirring the pot, he told me that the secret of good plov was patience. 'Never hurry the onions,' he said. 'They must turn golden slowly.' I peeled onions for two hours and cried the whole time.

On Friday the women made samsa and sweets. My grandmother, who is eighty, made the dough because nobody else could make it as thin as she could. I tried to help, but my samsas were bigger and uglier than hers, so she gave me an easier job: I put raisins and nuts on the plates. In the evening the neighbours brought chairs and tables, and the men put up a big tent in the yard because the weather forecast said it might rain.

The wedding began at five o'clock on Saturday. Madina looked beautiful in a red dress, and her husband Jasur was so nervous that he dropped his hat twice. When the guests sat down, the waiters brought salads, bread, fruit and tea first. The plov arrived at seven. People said it was the best they had ever eaten, and Rustam smiled proudly.

I was very tired at the end of the night, but I was happy. I have learned that a good feast needs many hands, a lot of time and a cook who is never in a hurry. Next year my brother is getting married, and I have already promised to peel the onions again.

items.prompt: Where did the writer find the notebook?
items.answer: In a box under the bed
items.passage:
Last month I found my grandmother's old notebook in a box under her bed. Inside there were forty recipes written by hand in blue ink, and one of them was called 'Winter lentil soup with lemon'. I had never made lentil soup before, but I was hungry and curious, so I decided to try it on Sunday.

First I went to the shop near our house. I needed red lentils, two carrots, one onion, garlic, a lemon and some cumin. The shopkeeper, Mr Anvar, told me that red lentils cook faster than green ones, which was useful to know. I paid six thousand som for the lentils and went home.

At home I washed the lentils and cut the vegetables. My little sister Zarina wanted to help, so she cut the carrots. She was cutting them very slowly, and the pieces were different sizes, but I said nothing. Then I fried the onion and garlic in a little oil for five minutes. The kitchen smelled wonderful. I added the carrots, the lentils, the cumin and four cups of water, and I cooked everything for twenty-five minutes.

The notebook said that I should add the lemon juice at the end. I did that, but I put in too much, and the soup was very sour. I was disappointed, but Zarina had a clever idea. She added a spoon of sugar and a little more salt, and the soup became much better. 'Now it's perfect,' she said.

We ate the soup with warm bread, and my parents loved it. My father said it tasted exactly like his mother's soup, and he had tears in his eyes. After dinner I called my grandmother in Fergana and told her about it. She laughed and said that she always used only half a lemon. Next time I will follow her advice.

Now I want to cook one recipe from the notebook every Sunday. I have already chosen the next one: a pumpkin pie from 1985. I hope it will be easier than the soup was.
options: In a box under the bed

items.prompt: How long had the family lived in the old flat?
items.passage:
In August my family moved from a small flat in Chilonzor to a bigger one in Yunusabad. We had lived in the old flat for nine years, so there was a lot to pack. My mother started two weeks before the move, and she wrote a list on the fridge. By the last week the list had sixty things on it.

On the moving day, a lorry arrived at eight o'clock. Two strong men, Sardor and Alisher, carried the sofa and the wardrobe down the stairs. The lift in our old building was broken, and we lived on the fifth floor, so it was hard work. My father said that he would never again buy such a heavy wardrobe. I carried the boxes of books, and my arms hurt for two days.

The new flat is on the second floor and has three rooms. It is much brighter than the old one because the windows face the south. I have my own bedroom for the first time, and my younger brother Temur has a small room next to mine. He is happy because he can play loud music without bothering anybody, although my mother says that he can't do that after nine o'clock in the evening.

There were some problems, of course. On the first night, we couldn't find the box with the plates, so we ate dinner from paper cups. The next day, the internet didn't work, and a technician came on Wednesday to fix it. Our neighbour, an old lady called Mrs Nilufar, brought us a cake and said we were welcome. She also told us where to find the best bakery and the nearest pharmacy.

I miss my old friends, but I have already made a new one. His name is Kamol, and he lives in the flat below ours. He is learning to play the guitar, and we are going to start a small band. Moving was tiring, but I think the new flat will be a good place to live.

items.prompt: Where was the empty yard?
items.passage:
Last spring our school started a garden project. Our teacher, Ms Karimova, said that the empty yard behind the gym was too ugly and that we could turn it into a green place. At first, nobody believed her, because the ground was hard and full of stones. But in April, thirty students from class seven agreed to help, and we began to work every Friday after lessons.

The first job was to clean the yard. We collected a lot of rubbish: old bottles, bags and even a broken chair. Then the caretaker, Mr Botir, brought a small tractor and dug the soil. We made six long beds and put a fence around them so that the school cats couldn't walk on the plants. I was in the group that built the fence, and I hit my thumb with a hammer twice.

In May we planted the seeds. Some students chose tomatoes and cucumbers, and others chose flowers. I planted carrots and herbs such as mint and dill. We watered the beds every morning before school, and we made a timetable so that everybody had a turn. My turn was on Tuesdays.

In June there was a problem. It was so hot that the small plants almost died. We needed more water, but the school tap was far from the garden. Then a girl called Shahlo had an idea. She asked her father, who is a plumber, to help us, and he put a long hose and a new tap near the beds. After that, the plants grew much faster.

In September we had our first harvest. We picked about forty kilos of vegetables and gave half of them to the school kitchen. The cook made a big salad for the whole school, and everybody said it was delicious. Now we are planning to plant apple trees next year. Ms Karimova says it will take five years before we can eat the apples, but we are patient.

items.prompt: How long has Grandfather lived in the mahalla?
items.passage:
My grandfather Hakim has lived in the same old mahalla in Bukhara for seventy years. Last weekend I stayed with him, and he showed me the streets where he played as a child. It was a fascinating day, and I want to write about it.

The streets in the mahalla are narrow, and the houses are made of clay and wood. In the middle there is a small square with a pond and a big mulberry tree. Grandfather says that the tree is more than three hundred years old. 'When I was a boy,' he told me, 'all the old men sat under this tree every evening and drank tea. They talked about the weather, the harvest and the neighbours' children.' Now the tree is still there, but the old men are fewer, and many young families have moved to modern districts.

We visited the little mosque, the bakery and the public bath, which is called a hammom. The baker, Mr Said, was making hot non in a clay oven. He gave me a piece, and it was the tastiest bread I have ever eaten. He told me that his family had worked in the bakery for five generations. Then we walked to a small workshop where a man called Fayzullo made copper pots. The noise was loud, but I liked watching him work.

The mahalla has changed in some ways. There are now two cafes for tourists, and a few houses have become small hotels. Grandfather isn't happy about this, because the street is noisier than before and the rents are higher. But he also says that the tourists bring money, and the neighbours can repair their old walls.

In the evening we sat under the mulberry tree and drank green tea. Grandfather said that a mahalla is not only houses; it is people who help one another. When his wife was ill ten years ago, all the neighbours brought food to the house. I will never forget that story. I think I will visit him more often.
