items.prompt: Where is the writer's village?
items.passage:
Last April a big flood hit our village, Qumqo'rg'on, in the south of Uzbekistan. I was fourteen at that time, and I will remember those three days for the rest of my life.

It had been raining for a week in the mountains, and the river near our village was getting higher every day. On Monday night, at about eleven o'clock, my father heard a strange noise. He looked out of the window and saw water in the street. We woke up quickly, took our documents and some warm clothes, and went to the school, which is on a hill. Many neighbours were already there. The headmaster, Mr Davron, had opened all the classrooms and made tea for everybody.

We slept on the floor that night. In the morning we could see our street from the school window. The water was almost one metre deep, and some people were moving through it in small boats. Soldiers and volunteers arrived from the city with food, blankets and drinking water. A young doctor, Dr Feruza, looked after the children who had colds. She worked for almost twenty hours without sleep.

On Wednesday the rain stopped, and the water began to go down. We returned home on Thursday. Our house was wet and dirty, and the carpets were ruined, but luckily the walls were strong. Our neighbour, an old man called Karim, lost his small garden and two sheep. Everybody helped him, and the villagers gave him a new sheep a month later.

The government decided to build a higher wall along the river this year. Engineers say that it will be finished in autumn, and it will protect us from floods in the future. I am proud of how the people in my village behaved. Nobody was selfish, and everyone shared what they had. My father says that a flood shows who your real friends are, and now I understand what he means.

items.prompt: Where does Mr Nodir work?
items.answer: In a nature reserve in the Tien Shan mountains
items.passage:
Last Thursday our class listened to a talk by a wildlife ranger called Mr Nodir, who works in a nature reserve in the Tien Shan mountains. He spoke about animals that are in danger, and I made notes because I wanted to remember everything.

Mr Nodir started with the snow leopard. He said that there are only about four thousand of them left in the wild, and only a few live in Uzbekistan. They are very shy animals, and people almost never see them. Rangers use special cameras that take pictures when something moves. Last year the cameras in his reserve took photographs of three different leopards.

Then he talked about the saiga antelope, an animal with a strange, big nose. In the past, millions of saigas lived in the steppe. Then hunters killed too many of them, and in some years a sickness killed thousands more. Now the number is growing again because the countries of Central Asia are protecting them together.

The third animal was the Bukhara deer, which lives near rivers in the desert forests. Fifty years ago there were fewer than three hundred of them. Today there are about a thousand, and the rangers move some deer to new places so that the herds are safer.

At the end of the talk, a boy asked what we can do. Mr Nodir said that we don't need to be rangers. We can use less plastic, never buy products made from wild animals, and tell our friends about these problems. He also asked us to visit nature reserves with our families, because the money from tickets helps to pay for the cameras and the food for the animals.

I left the classroom with a new idea. In the summer I am going to visit the reserve with my brother and take photographs of the mountains, but never of the leopards, because I suppose they will not let me see them.
options: In a nature reserve in the Tien Shan mountains

items.prompt: Who had the idea for Recycling Day?
items.passage:
Last Saturday our neighbourhood had its first Recycling Day. The idea came from a young woman called Sevara, who lives in our building and works for an environmental group. She put posters in all the entrances two weeks before, and on Saturday morning more than a hundred people came to the yard of School Number Fifteen.

There were five big containers in the yard, and each had a colour and a sign. The blue one was for paper, the green one for glass, the yellow one for plastic, the grey one for metal cans, and the red one for old batteries. Sevara explained that batteries are dangerous, and they must never go into a normal bin. I didn't know that before, and I felt a bit embarrassed because we had thrown away at least ten batteries at home.

My brother Aziz and I brought two big bags of newspapers and a box of plastic bottles. A volunteer weighed them and wrote the numbers in a notebook. In total, we brought nine kilos of paper and three kilos of plastic. For every five kilos, we received a small paper bag with flower seeds. I got marigolds, and Aziz got sunflowers.

The event was more popular than the organisers expected. By noon the paper container was full, and a lorry came to take it away. In total, people brought four hundred and twenty kilos of rubbish. items.prompt: What time does the market open?
items.passage:
Every Sunday morning my aunt Barno takes me to the street market near the old railway station in Tashkent. It opens at six o'clock, and she says that we must arrive early because the best fruit finishes quickly.

The market is long and narrow, and it is always full of people and noise. On the left side, sellers have tables with vegetables: red tomatoes, green peppers, big purple aubergines and bunches of fresh herbs. On the right side there are fruit stalls. In October you can buy sweet grapes, heavy melons and pomegranates from Kitab. A seller called Mr Ergash always shouts, 'Cheaper than yesterday!' even when the price is the same. My aunt always laughs at him and then buys half a kilo of grapes.

At the end of the street there is the part I like best, where they sell old things. You can find books, coins, radios and a lot of strange objects. Last Sunday I bought a small brass bell for ten thousand som. The seller, an old woman, wanted fifteen thousand, but my aunt told me to ask for a lower price. 'In a market you must always bargain,' she said. I tried, and the woman agreed to ten thousand. I was very pleased with myself.

After shopping we have breakfast at a small tea house. We usually order hot samsa and a pot of green tea. A kind waiter, Jahongir, already knows our table, and he brings us extra bread with honey. We sit for about an hour and watch people go by. My aunt says that a market is the best place to learn about a city, because there you can meet everybody: students, grandmothers, farmers and even tourists with big cameras.

When we go home, our bags are heavy, but my aunt's face is happy. Next Sunday I'm going to look for an old map, because my aunt says there is usually a man who sells them near the last table.

items.prompt: What is the writer going to look for next Sunday?
items.passage:
Every Sunday morning my aunt Barno takes me to the street market near the old railway station in Tashkent. It opens at six o'clock, and she says that we must arrive early because the best fruit finishes quickly.

The market is long and narrow, and it is always full of people and noise. On the left side, sellers have tables with vegetables: red tomatoes, green peppers, big purple aubergines and bunches of fresh herbs. On the right side there are fruit stalls. In October you can buy sweet grapes, heavy melons and pomegranates from Kitab. A seller called Mr Ergash always shouts, 'Cheaper than yesterday!' even when the price is the same. My aunt always laughs at him and then buys half a kilo of grapes.

At the end of the street there is the part I like best, where they sell old things. You can find books, coins, radios and a lot of strange objects. Last Sunday I bought a small brass bell for ten thousand som. The seller, an old woman, wanted fifteen thousand, but my aunt told me to ask for a lower price. 'In a market you must always bargain,' she said. I tried, and the woman agreed to ten thousand. I was very pleased with myself.

After shopping we have breakfast at a small tea house. We usually order hot samsa and a pot of green tea. A kind waiter, Jahongir, already knows our table, and he brings us extra bread with honey. We sit for about an hour and watch people go by. My aunt says that a market is the best place to learn about a city, because there you can meet everybody: students, grandmothers, farmers and even tourists with big cameras.

When we go home, our bags are heavy, but my aunt's face is happy. Next Sunday I'm going to look for an old map, because my aunt says there is usually a man who sells them near the last table.

items.prompt: When does the village celebrate Navruz?
items.passage:
Every year on the twenty-first of March, my village celebrates Navruz, the spring festival. This year I was in charge of one small part of it for the first time, and I was both excited and a little frightened.

The preparation began a week before the holiday. The women of the village met at my grandmother's house to cook sumalak, a sweet dish made from wheat. It is very special because it has to be cooked for a whole night. Twelve women took turns to stir the huge pot, and they sang old songs to stay awake. I was allowed to stir for twenty minutes, and my arm hurt for the rest of the evening. In the morning the sumalak was thick, brown and delicious.

On the festival day the whole village gathered in the big field near the school. The weather was warm and sunny, which was lucky because last year it rained. Children ran around with colourful ribbons, and the men put up a stage for the musicians. Then there were competitions. The boys had a race, and the girls had a skipping competition. My cousin Gulbahor won the girls' contest, and she got a prize: a set of beautiful pencils.

My job was to show visitors the exhibition of handmade things in the school hall. There were carpets, embroidered caps and wooden spoons. An old woman, Mrs Halima, explained how she made her carpet in six months. Some visitors from Tashkent bought several things, and I felt proud of our village.

In the evening we lit a big fire, and everybody sat around it and ate sumalak and sweets. The teacher read a poem about spring, and a boy played the dutar. I went to bed very late, but I wasn't tired at all.

Next year I would like to help with the music. My grandmother says that if I practise every day, I may be able to play the drum by then.

items.prompt: Where does Lola work?
items.passage:
Last month my friend Lola started to look for a flat in Tashkent. She had just got a job at a bank, and her office is in the city centre, so she wanted to live somewhere close. She asked me to help, and I spent three Saturdays going with her to see different places.

The first flat was in a modern building near the metro. It had two rooms, a new kitchen and a nice balcony, and the rent was five hundred dollars a month. Lola loved it, but it was too expensive for her, because she earns only seven hundred. 'I can't pay more than three hundred and fifty,' she said sadly. The agent, a polite man called Murod, told us that cheaper flats are usually further from the centre.

The second flat was cheaper, only three hundred dollars, but it was on the ninth floor of an old building, and the lift didn't work. The rooms were dark, and the bathroom smelled of damp. I told Lola that she shouldn't take it, and she agreed immediately. We were both tired when we left.

On the third Saturday we saw a small flat in a quiet street near a park. It had one room, a little kitchen and a window with a view of big trees. The landlady, Mrs Dilbar, was a retired teacher. She asked Lola many questions: where she worked, whether she had pets, and if she liked loud music. Lola answered everything honestly. Mrs Dilbar said that the rent was three hundred and forty dollars and that the flat would be available from the first of December.

Lola signed the contract the next day. She will need to take a bus for fifteen minutes to reach her office, but she says that it's better than living in a noisy place. We have already planned to paint the walls light blue. I promised to help her move, and in return she has promised to cook me dinner every Friday.

items.prompt: When did the writer start working at the shelter?
items.passage:
Since January I have been a volunteer at an animal shelter on the edge of our city. I go there every Wednesday and Sunday, and I have learned more about animals in these months than in all my years at school.

The shelter was opened five years ago by a veterinarian called Dr Shirin. At the moment there are about sixty dogs and thirty cats living there. Most of them were found in the street, and some were hurt or ill. Dr Shirin says that the saddest cases are the animals that people left on the roads because they didn't want them any more. She often tells us that a pet is not a toy, and that it needs time, money and love.

My work begins at nine o'clock. First I clean the cages and give the animals fresh water. Then I feed them, and after that I take the dogs for a walk in the field behind the shelter. My favourite dog is a young brown puppy called Bonu. He was found under a bridge in the winter, and he was so thin that he could hardly stand. Now he is much stronger, and he runs faster than any other dog in the group.

Sometimes families come to choose a new pet. Dr Shirin always asks them many questions before she lets them take an animal. She wants to be sure that the family has enough space and is able to take care of it. Last month a boy called Ilyos took a grey cat, and he sent us a photograph a week later. The cat was sleeping on his bed, and he looked very happy.

The shelter needs help because it doesn't have much money. We organise a small sale of cakes every second Saturday, and we collect old blankets and towels. I would love to adopt Bonu myself, but my mother is afraid of dogs. I am trying to change her mind, and I think that after she meets him, she will love him.

items.prompt: How far is the lake from Tashkent?
items.answer: Three hours by car and two hours on foot
items.passage:
Last summer my uncle Rustam took me and my cousin Anvar to a small mountain lake called Kul-Tosh. It is about three hours from Tashkent by car, and then you must walk for two more hours. Uncle Rustam said that the walk was worth it, and he was right.

We left home at five o'clock in the morning. The road was empty and quiet, and the sun was just coming up when we reached the foot of the mountains. We parked the car near a small village and started walking with heavy rucksacks. Each of us carried water, bread, apples, a warm jacket and a raincoat. The path was steep at first, and Anvar, who is two years younger than me, complained that his legs were tired. But after an hour we saw a beautiful valley with yellow flowers, and he forgot about his legs.

We stopped for lunch next to a fast, cold stream. He also told us never to leave rubbish in the mountains. 'Take everything back with you,' he said, 'because nature is not a bin.' We ate our bread and apples and drank the clear water from the stream, which was the sweetest I have ever tasted.

At about two o'clock in the afternoon we finally arrived at the lake. It was bigger than I had imagined, and its water was a deep, dark blue. High snowy peaks stood all around, and their reflection was in the water. It was so quiet that we could hear birds on the other side. The water was too cold for swimming, but I put my feet in, and it took my breath away.

We stayed for one hour and took a lot of photographs. On the way back the weather suddenly changed, and it began to rain, so we put on our raincoats. We got home very late, tired and wet, but extremely happy. Uncle Rustam promised to take us again next summer, and this time we will stay in a tent overnight.
options: Three hours by car and two hours on foot

items.prompt: How did the students travel?
items.passage:
In April our class went on a two-day trip to the Kyzylkum desert. Our geography teacher, Mr Oybek, organised everything, and thirty students and three teachers travelled in two big buses. We left school at seven o'clock in the morning and drove for almost six hours.

When we got out of the bus, I was surprised. I had expected a flat, empty place, but the desert was full of life. There were low bushes, small flowers and many different birds. Our guide, an old man called Mr Ruzi, told us that April is the best month for visiting because it isn't too hot yet. In July the temperature can be above forty-five degrees, and nobody can stay outside at noon.

In the afternoon we rode camels. Mine was called Sultan, and it was much taller than I had thought. At first I was afraid, because the camel stood up very suddenly. But after ten minutes I got used to it, and I enjoyed the slow walk over the red sand. Mr Ruzi said that camels can live without water for two weeks, but that they drink a hundred litres at once when they find it.

We spent the night in a yurt camp. In the evening we ate shurpa and bread around a fire, and a local singer played the dutar. After dinner Mr Oybek showed us the stars. He pointed out the Milky Way, and the girls took photographs until their phones ran out of battery.

The night was cold, and I was glad that I had brought a warm sweater. In the morning I woke up at five, because I wanted to see the sunrise. The sand turned pink and then gold, and it was perhaps the most beautiful moment of my life.

On the way home everybody was sleepy. Mr Oybek asked us to write a short report about the trip. I think I will write about the stars, and I will certainly go back to the desert when I'm older.

items.prompt: When is the farmers' market open?
items.answer: On Saturdays from eight to one
items.passage:
Every Saturday from eight to one o'clock there is a farmers' market in the square near my house. It started three years ago, when a group of farmers from the Fergana Valley decided to sell their products directly to people in the city. My mother says that this is the best idea the city has ever had.

The most popular stall belongs to Mr Olim, who sells apples. He has eleven kinds, and he lets you taste each one before you buy. The red ones are sweet, and the green ones are sour. Last week I bought two kilos of the sweet apples, and my mother made a delicious pie. Mr Olim told me that his apples are fresher than the ones in supermarkets because he picks them the day before the market.

Next to Mr Olim there is a woman called Mrs Zuhra, who sells honey and cheese. Her honey is a bit more expensive than honey in a shop, but it is natural and she keeps the bees herself. She has forty hives in a village near Namangan. She showed me a photograph of them, and she explained that bees need clean air and many flowers. When I asked whether bees are dangerous, she laughed and said that they are kind if you are kind to them.

There is also a small stall with vegetables grown without chemicals. The young farmer, Behzod, studied agriculture at university, and now he works on his father's land. He says that these vegetables don't look perfect, but they taste better than the beautiful ones from the supermarket. I think he is right, because his carrots are crunchy and very sweet.

My favourite part of the market is the corner with music. On most Saturdays an old man plays the accordion, and children dance next to him.

I think we should have more markets like this one. They bring fresh food and help small farmers, and they make the city a friendlier place to live.
options: On Saturdays from eight to one
On Sundays from six to ten
